s: Herodotus introduces the Scythian vapour bath as what they do after a burial: 'having buried, the Scythians cleanse themselves in this way'.

src.l: Herodotus, 1921, Herodotus, Histories, Books 3-4 (Loeb, Greek pages)
src.q: θάψαντες δὲ οἱ Σκύθαι καθαίρονται τρόπῳ τοιῷδε.

src.l: Herodotus, 1921, Herodotus, Histories, Books 3-4 (Loeb, Greek pages)
src.q: After the burial, the Scythians purify themselves in the following way
src.qo: θάψαντες δὲ οἱ Σκύθαι καθαίρονται τρόπῳ τοιῷδε.

s: Herodotus says that for the body the Scythians set up three poles leaning together, stretch woollen felts round them as tightly closed as possible, and throw stones glowing from the fire into a trough set in the middle.

src.l: Herodotus, 1921, Herodotus, Histories, Books 3-4 (Loeb, Greek pages)
src.q: ἐπεὰν ξύλα στήσωσι τρία ἐς ἄλληλα κεκλιμένα, περὶ ταῦτα πίλους εἰρινέους περιτείνουσι, συμφράξαντες δὲ ὡς μάλιστα λίθους ἐκ πυρὸς διαφανέας ἐσβάλλουσι ἐς σκάφην κειμένην ἐν μέσῳ τῶν ξύλων τε καὶ τῶν πίλων.

src.l: Herodotus, 1921, Herodotus, Histories, Books 3-4 (Loeb, Greek pages)
src.q: they set up three poles leaning against each other and stretch woolen felts around them, closing them as tightly as possible; then they throw stones made red-hot from a fire into a basin that sits in the middle of the poles and felts.
src.qo: ἐπεὰν ξύλα στήσωσι τρία ἐς ἄλληλα κεκλιμένα, περὶ ταῦτα πίλους εἰρινέους περιτείνουσι, συμφράξαντες δὲ ὡς μάλιστα λίθους ἐκ πυρὸς διαφανέας ἐσβάλλουσι ἐς σκάφην κειμένην ἐν μέσῳ τῶν ξύλων τε καὶ τῶν πίλων.

s: Herodotus says that what is thrown on the glowing stones smoulders and gives off so much vapour that no Greek vapour bath (pyria) could surpass it.

src.l: Herodotus, 1921, Herodotus, Histories, Books 3-4 (Loeb, Greek pages)
src.q: τὸ δὲ θυμιᾶται ἐπιβαλλόμενον καὶ ἀτμίδα παρέχεται τοσαύτην ὥστε Ἑλληνικὴ οὐδεμία ἄν μιν πυρίη ἀποκρατήσειε.

src.l: Herodotus, 1921, Herodotus, Histories, Books 3-4 (Loeb, Greek pages)
src.q: then the seed smolders and sends forth such a vapor that no Greek vapor-bath could surpass it.
src.qo: τὸ δὲ θυμιᾶται ἐπιβαλλόμενον καὶ ἀτμίδα παρέχεται τοσαύτην ὥστε Ἑλληνικὴ οὐδεμία ἄν μιν πυρίη ἀποκρατήσειε.

s: Herodotus says the Scythians, delighted by the vapour bath, howl, and that this is for them in place of a bath (loutron), because they do not wash the body with water at all.

src.l: Herodotus, 1921, Herodotus, Histories, Books 3-4 (Loeb, Greek pages)
src.q: οἱ δὲ Σκύθαι ἀγάμενοι τῇ πυρίῃ ὠρύονται. τοῦτό σφι ἀντὶ λουτροῦ ἐστι· οὐ γὰρ δὴ λούονται ὕδατι τὸ παράπαν τὸ σῶμα.

src.l: Herodotus, 1921, Herodotus, Histories, Books 3-4 (Loeb, Greek pages)
src.q: The Scythians, delighted with this vapor-bath, howl with joy. This serves them as a bath, for they never wash their bodies with water at all.
src.qo: οἱ δὲ Σκύθαι ἀγάμενοι τῇ πυρίῃ ὠρύονται. τοῦτό σφι ἀντὶ λουτροῦ ἐστι· οὐ γὰρ δὴ λούονται ὕδατι τὸ παράπαν τὸ σῶμα.

s: Herodotus adds that the Scythian women pound cypress, cedar and frankincense wood on a rough stone with water, plaster the paste over the whole body and face, and when they take it off the next day are 'clean and shining'.

src.l: Herodotus, 1921, Herodotus, Histories, Books 3-4 (Loeb, Greek pages)
src.q: καὶ ἅμα μὲν εὐωδίη σφέας ἀπὸ τούτου ἴσχει, ἅμα δὲ ἀπαιρέουσαι τῇ δευτέρῃ ἡμέρῃ τὴν καταπλαστὺν γίνονται καθαραὶ καὶ λαμπραί.

src.l: Herodotus, 1921, Herodotus, Histories, Books 3-4 (Loeb, Greek pages)
src.q: This gives them a pleasant scent, and when they strip off the plaster on the second day, they are clean and their skin is shining.
src.qo: καὶ ἅμα μὲν εὐωδίη σφέας ἀπὸ τούτου ἴσχει, ἅμα δὲ ἀπαιρέουσαι τῇ δευτέρῃ ἡμέρῃ τὴν καταπλαστὺν γίνονται καθαραὶ καὶ λαμπραί.

s: Olaus Magnus opens his chapter on baths by saying that in most places, above all Italy, baths were mostly devised for pleasure, but that nowhere in the world is their use so necessary as in the northern kingdoms.

src.loc: Book 15, ch. 35, printed p. 527, scan p. 616

src.q: The soul is a river, whose holy bathing place is self-restraint, whose water is truth, and whose banks are moral character and waves are virtues. Perform your ritual bathing in that, O son of Pandu, for the inner self is not purified by water.
src.qo: आत्मा नदी संयमपुण्यतीर्थाः सत्योदका शीलत टादयोर्मिः। तत्राभिषेकं कुरु पाण्डुपुत्र न वारिणा शु द्ध्यति चान्तरात्मा

s: The first verse the Tengyur treatise ascribes to Vyāsa (I am the river, truth the water, do your bathing there, the inner self is not made clean by water) is the same verse that the Hitopadesha quotes in Sanskrit, so the Buddhist critic and the Hindu story-book draw on one piece of brahmanical self-criticism.

s: The Tang encyclopedia Chuxue ji quotes the Han writer Zhang Heng's "Rhapsody on the Hot Spring" (溫泉賦), whose closing lines say that when the six qi fall into disorder and there is pestilence, the hot spring flows to carry off filth and clear away what is harsh and noxious, and so preserves life.

s: In the preface quoted by the Chuxue ji, Zhang Heng says he went to Mount Li, saw the hot spring and bathed in the "divine well" (神井); the rhapsody then describes people from far regions hurrying there, men and women gathering like fish scales.

s: The Qing encyclopedia Yuanjian leihan quotes the old "Record of the Three Qin" (辛氏三秦記): by old report one could enter the Mount Li hot spring only after sacrificing the three victims, and it could then remove disease.

s: The same tradition, as quoted in the Yuanjian leihan and the Gezhi jingyuan, explains the Mount Li spring by a story: the First Emperor of Qin consorted with a divine woman and offended her; she spat on him and sores broke out; he begged pardon in fear, and she brought forth the hot spring to wash them away.

src.q: In the past, when Qin Shi Huang was traveling with a divine woman and offended her, she spat on him and sores grew on his body. The Emperor was frightened and apologized, so the divine woman produced a hot spring to wash them away.

s: The Gezhi jingyuan quotes the Ming traveller Du Mu's account of Mount Li: the hot-spring pool there was called the "official pool" because only persons of rank might bathe in it, and to its left a spring called the "mixed pool" was for bathing the common people.

s: The "Scripture on Bathing Body and Mind" (沐浴身心經), as quoted in Zhou Shouzhong's Yangsheng leizuan and in the Yunji qiqian, assigns each of five fragrant bath ingredients a power: angelica drives out the Three Corpses, peach bark wards off evil qi, cypress leaf brings down true immortals, lingling herb gathers the numinous sages, and costus removes filth and summons the true ones.

src.q: For bathing, five varieties of fragrant decoctions are used. First is baizhi, which can expel the Three Corpses. Second is peach bark, which can ward off evil influences. Third is cypress leaves, which can bring down true immortals. Fourth is linglingxiang, which can gather divine sages. Fifth is qingmuxiang, which can dispel defilements and summon the true celestial spirits.

s: The same "Scripture on Bathing Body and Mind", quoted in the Yunji qiqian, defines two baths: to be clean within is an empty heart without stain, to be clean without is the body's dirt wholly removed; it adds that the one who prepares the hot water gains merit without measure.

s: The Yunji qiqian gives a calendar of "auspicious days for bathing": one day and hour in each month with its result, for example the tenth of the first month at the hour when people settle, which makes the teeth firm, and the eighteenth of the tenth month at first cockcrow, which gives long life; it explains that on these days the moon lodges in the Eastern Well and one meets the immortals.

s: The Yunji qiqian sets two Daoist authorities side by side on how often to bathe: the Lady of Purple Tenuity says it is the nature of the hun soul not to want frequent bathing, while the Lady of the Southern Peak (cited from the Zhen'gao) says one cannot bathe too often, since frequent bathing scours away the corpse-stench so that true qi comes in.

s: On the same Analects line, Zhu Xi's commentary in the Sishu zuanshu glosses "bathe" as washing (盥濯) and identifies it with the lustration (祓除) of the third-month Shangsi festival; the appended discussion reports that Han Yu and Li Ao thought naked river-bathing improper and emended the word.

s: The Kojiki has Izanagi judge the water before he washes: the upper reach is too fast and the lower too weak, so he dives in the middle reach; the first gods that come into being as he rinses are two "gods of bending ill", which the text says arose from the filth of the defiled land.

s: In the public baths at Baden, where a partition divides men from women, Poggio found it laughable to see old and young women enter the water naked before men's eyes, and wondered at the simplicity of people who neither look at these things nor suspect or speak any evil.

src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 313 (printed 298)

src.q: It is ridiculous to see old women, decrepit and at the same time younger ones, naked, entering the waters in the eyes of men, showing their private parts and buttocks to the men. ... with myself I admired the simplicity of these people, who neither turn their eyes toward these things, nor suspect or speak anything of evil.

s: In the private house baths at Baden, Poggio says, men and women share the bath with a board partition pierced by many small windows through which they drink together, talk, see and touch each other; above are walkways where people stand to watch and chat.

src.q: At uero balnea in domibus priuatorum perpolita ſunt, & ipſa uiris fœminisq; cōmunia, tabulata quædam hæc ſecernūt. Et in his feneſtrellæ perplures dimiſſæ, quibus & una potare, ſimul & colloqui, & utrinq; uidere & attractare queant, ut eorum frequens eſt conſuetudo. Hæc deſuper fiunt deambulatoria, in quibus conſpiciendi & confabulandi cauſa homines conſiſtunt.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 313 (printed 298)
src.q: And in these are many small windows, through which they are able to drink together, and to converse at the same time, and to see and touch one another on both sides, as is their frequent custom. ... These are made above as promenades, in which men stand for the sake of seeing and conversing.
src.qo: At uero balnea in domibus priuatorum perpolita ſunt, & ipſa uiris fœminisq; cōmunia, tabulata quædam hæc ſecernūt. Et in his feneſtrellæ perplures dimiſſæ, quibus & una potare, ſimul & colloqui, & utrinq; uidere & attractare queant, ut eorum frequens eſt conſuetudo. Hæc deſuper fiunt deambulatoria, in quibus conſpiciendi & confabulandi cauſa homines conſiſtunt.

s: Poggio reports that bathers at Baden often dine in the water from shared contributions at a table floating on it; invited once, he paid his share but would not join, he says not from shame but because he did not know the language.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 314 (printed 299)
src.q: In ipſis aquis ſæpe de ſymbolis edūt, cōpoſita meſa deſuper aqua natante, quib. uiros aſſiſtere cōſueuerunt. Nos quidā ea in domo qua lauabamur, ſemel uocati ſumus ad eā conſuetudinē. Ego uero ſymbolū cōtuli, intereſſe nolui licet etiā atq; etiā rogatus, nō permotus pudore qui pro ignauia habet ac ruſticitate, ſed inſcitia ſermōis.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 314 (printed 299)
src.q: In the waters themselves, they often dine from shared contributions, with a table arranged floating on top of the water ... I did not wish to attend, although I was asked again and again, not moved by a sense of shame—which is held to be a sign of cowardice and rusticity—but by a lack of knowledge of the language.
src.qo: In ipſis aquis ſæpe de ſymbolis edūt, cōpoſita meſa deſuper aqua natante, quib. uiros aſſiſtere cōſueuerunt. Nos quidā ea in domo qua lauabamur, ſemel uocati ſumus ad eā conſuetudinē. Ego uero ſymbolū cōtuli, intereſſe nolui licet etiā atq; etiā rogatus, nō permotus pudore qui pro ignauia habet ac ruſticitate, ſed inſcitia ſermōis.

s: Watching husbands see their wives touched by strangers without taking offence, Poggio says the people at Baden would have fitted Plato's republic, where all things are common, since without his teaching they are so ready for his sect.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 314 (printed 299)
src.q: Permirū eſt uidere qua ſimplicitate uiuāt, qua fide uidebāt uiri uxores ſuas a peregrinis tangi. Non cōmouebāt nō animū aduertebāt, omia in meliorē partē accipiūt. Nil eſt tā difficile quin eorū morib. facile fiat. Plane in politiā Platonis cōueniſſent, ut omnia eſſent cōmunia, cū & iam abſq; eius doctrina, tam prōpti in ipſius ſectā reperiant̃.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 314 (printed 299)
src.q: It is truly marvelous to see with what simplicity they live, with what trust the husbands saw their wives touched by strangers. ... They would clearly have fit into Plato’s Republic, that all things might be common, since even without his doctrine, they are found so ready for his very sect.
src.qo: Permirū eſt uidere qua ſimplicitate uiuāt, qua fide uidebāt uiri uxores ſuas a peregrinis tangi. Non cōmouebāt nō animū aduertebāt, omia in meliorē partē accipiūt. Nil eſt tā difficile quin eorū morib. facile fiat. Plane in politiā Platonis cōueniſſent, ut omnia eſſent cōmunia, cū & iam abſq; eius doctrina, tam prōpti in ipſius ſectā reperiant̃.

s: Poggio says the bathers at Baden enter the baths three or four times a day and spend most of the day there singing, drinking and dancing, and that women jokingly beg alms from the men looking down from above.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 314 (printed 299)
src.q: Quotidie ter aut quater balnea intrant, maiorē in his diei partē agētes, partim cantādo, partim potando, partim choreas exercendo. ... Mos eſt mulieribus, ut cum uiri eas deſuper proſpectant, iocandi gratia ſtipem petere.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 314 (printed 299)
src.q: Daily they enter the baths three or four times, spending the greater part of the day in them, partly by singing, partly by drinking, partly by dancing. ... It is the custom for women, when men look down upon them from above, to ask for a gift for the sake of joking.
src.qo: Quotidie ter aut quater balnea intrant, maiorē in his diei partē agētes, partim cantādo, partim potando, partim choreas exercendo. ... Mos eſt mulieribus, ut cum uiri eas deſuper proſpectant, iocandi gratia ſtipem petere.

s: Poggio calls the company at Baden a school of the Epicurean sect and says he believes this is the place where the first man was created, which the Hebrews call (as printed) Gamedon, the garden of pleasure.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 315 (printed 300)
src.q: Hos autem retuli, ut comprehendas quanta sit hæc scola Epicureæ factionis. Atq; hunc illum lo esse credo, in quo primū hominē creatum, quem Gamedon Hebræi uocant, hoc est hortum uoluptatis.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 315 (printed 300)
src.q: I have related these, however, so that you might understand how great this school of the Epicurean faction is. And I believe this to be that place where the first man was created, whom the Hebrews call Gamedon, that is, the garden of pleasure.
src.qo: Hos autem retuli, ut comprehendas quanta sit hæc scola Epicureæ factionis. Atq; hunc illum lo esse credo, in quo primū hominē creatum, quem Gamedon Hebræi uocant, hoc est hortum uoluptatis.

s: Poggio says he believes no baths in the world are better suited to women's fertility, and that a countless crowd comes to Baden from two hundred miles away less for health than for pleasure, many feigning bodily illness when the trouble is in the mind.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 315 (printed 300)
src.q: Nec ego esse ulla in orbe terrarum balnea credam ad fœcunditatem mulierū magis accommodata. ... Innumerabilis multitudo nobilium & ignobilium, ducenta milium passuum huc uenientiū, non tam ualitudinis causa, quam uoluptatis ... Multæ corporum simulantur egritudines, cum animo laborent.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 315 (printed 300)
src.q: Nor would I believe there to be any baths in the round world more suited to the fertility of women. ... an innumerable multitude of noble and ignoble, coming here from two hundred miles away, not so much for the sake of health as for pleasure ... Many illnesses of the body are feigned, while they suffer in their minds.
src.qo: Nec ego esse ulla in orbe terrarum balnea credam ad fœcunditatem mulierū magis accommodata. ... Innumerabilis multitudo nobilium & ignobilium, ducenta milium passuum huc uenientiū, non tam ualitudinis causa, quam uoluptatis ... Multæ corporum simulantur egritudines, cum animo laborent.

s: Poggio says that at Baden abbots, monks, friars and priests live with more licence than the rest, sometimes bathing together with women and dressing their hair with silk ribbons, all religion cast aside.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 315 (printed 300)
src.q: Hic abbates, monachi, fratres, & sacerdotes maiori licentia quàm cæteri uiuunt, & simul quandoq; cum mulieribus lauantes, sericis quoq; comas ornantes, omni religione abiecta.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 315 (printed 300)
src.q: Here abbots, monks, friars, and priests live with greater license than the rest, and sometimes bathing together with women, adorning their hair with silks, having cast aside all religion.
src.qo: Hic abbates, monachi, fratres, & sacerdotes maiori licentia quàm cæteri uiuunt, & simul quandoq; cum mulieribus lauantes, sericis quoq; comas ornantes, omni religione abiecta.

s: Poggio says the word for a jealous husband has no place among the people at Baden, and that he often envies their quiet and curses the perversity of his own countrymen who overturn heaven, earth and sea to dig out money.

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 316 (printed 301)
src.q: Itaq; nomen zelotypi, quod quasi omnes maritos oppressit, apud istos locum non habet. ... Inuideo persaepe istorum quieti, & nostras execror animi peruersitates, qui semper quaerimus, semper appetimus, qui coelum & terras & mare peruertimus ad pecunia eruendam

src.l: Poggio Bracciolini, 1538, Poggii Florentini Opera (Basel 1538)
src.loc: Letter to Niccoli on the baths, scan p. 316 (printed 301)
src.q: Thus, the name of "jealousy," which has oppressed almost all husbands, has no place among these people. ... I very often envy the peace of these people, and I execrate the perversities of our own minds—we who are always searching, always grasping, who turn heaven and earth and sea upside down to extract money
src.qo: Itaq; nomen zelotypi, quod quasi omnes maritos oppressit, apud istos locum non habet. ... Inuideo persaepe istorum quieti, & nostras execror animi peruersitates, qui semper quaerimus, semper appetimus, qui coelum & terras & mare peruertimus ad pecunia eruendam

s: Dryander (Bad Ems, 1541) says women often become pregnant after using the warm baths because the bathing has made them ready to conceive, adds that other causes may sometimes be at work since pleasure and joy at the wild baths are great, and calls what is healed in that way a cure 'per accidens'.

src.l: Johann Dryander, 1541, Vom Eymsser Bade was natur es in ihm hab
src.loc: Vom Eymsser Bade, scan p. 18
src.q: nach dem sie gebraucht haben die warmen bäder / bernacher schwanger werden ... dann das baden sie zu emp- fangen bereit gemacht hat. ... Dann der lust und die freude in wiltbädern groß ist ... Nu was off die weise durchs badt geheilet wirt / ist cura per acci- dens und nit anders.

src.l: Johann Dryander, 1541, Vom Eymsser Bade was natur es in ihm hab
src.loc: Vom Eymsser Bade, scan p. 18
src.q: after they have used the warm baths, thereafter become pregnant ... then the bathing has made them ready to conceive. ... For the pleasure and the joy in the wild baths is great ... Now what is healed in this way through the bath is cura per accidens and nothing else.
src.qo: nach dem sie gebraucht haben die warmen bäder / bernacher schwanger werden ... dann das baden sie zu emp- fangen bereit gemacht hat. ... Dann der lust und die freude in wiltbädern groß ist ... Nu was off die weise durchs badt geheilet wirt / ist cura per acci- dens und nit anders.

s: Dryander does not advise against going to the bath for the cure 'per accidens', but says that if good company and recreation of mind are all one wants they can be had elsewhere without crossing so many mountains at great cost, and that no one should go to a bath without first asking his physician.

src.l: Johann Dryander, 1541, Vom Eymsser Bade was natur es in ihm hab
src.loc: Vom Eymsser Bade, scan p. 18
src.q: Kansts aber auch anderswo / so du nur gute gesellschafft / unnd deines gemüts ergetzung hast / bekomen / mußt derhalben nit eben / mit gros- sen kosten / so viel berge ubersteigen ... Es soll keiner ins badt zihen / er habe dann seinem Medicum / oder einen gelerten der natürlichen dingen / gerathfraget

src.l: Johann Dryander, 1541, Vom Eymsser Bade was natur es in ihm hab
src.loc: Vom Eymsser Bade, scan p. 18
src.q: But if you can obtain this elsewhere, provided you only have good company and recreation of your mind, you do not have to climb so many mountains at great cost ... No one should travel to the bath unless he has asked his Medicum or someone learned in natural things
src.qo: Kansts aber auch anderswo / so du nur gute gesellschafft / unnd deines gemüts ergetzung hast / bekomen / mußt derhalben nit eben / mit gros- sen kosten / so viel berge ubersteigen ... Es soll keiner ins badt zihen / er habe dann seinem Medicum / oder einen gelerten der natürlichen dingen / gerathfraget

s: Fautsch's Latin poem on a thermal spring (his title places it in the lower tract of the Hercynian forest) says a divine power ('Numen') is in the spring and dispenses help by a hidden law, and tells of a gouty friend who vowed himself to the spring, fulfilled the vow, used the baths, and walked home leaving his crutches behind.

src.l: Johannes Fautsch, 1618, Schediasma quo duo famosissimi fontes in inferiori Hercyniae sylvae tractu scaturientes ... celebrantur
src.loc: Schediasma, scan p. 6
src.q: Numen inest fonti quod opem mirâ arte modoque Dispensat, nec se prodit nisi lege latente:

src.l: Johannes Fautsch, 1618, Schediasma quo duo famosissimi fontes in inferiori Hercyniae sylvae tractu scaturientes ... celebrantur
src.loc: Schediasma, scan p. 6
src.q: A divine presence resides within the spring, which distributes aid through wonderful art and manner, nor does it reveal itself except by a latent law:
src.qo: Numen inest fonti quod opem mirâ arte modoque Dispensat, nec se prodit nisi lege latente:

src.l: Johannes Fautsch, 1618, Schediasma quo duo famosissimi fontes in inferiori Hercyniae sylvae tractu scaturientes ... celebrantur
src.loc: Schediasma, scan p. 7
src.q: Se fonti huic uouit, votumque impleuit, & istis Vsus erat Thermis: ... Atque pedes patriam fulcris petit ille relictis.

src.l: Johannes Fautsch, 1618, Schediasma quo duo famosissimi fontes in inferiori Hercyniae sylvae tractu scaturientes ... celebrantur
src.loc: Schediasma, scan p. 7
src.q: He dedicated himself to this spring, fulfilled his vow, and used These thermal waters. ... And seeking his fatherland on foot, having left his supports behind.
src.qo: Se fonti huic uouit, votumque impleuit, & istis Vsus erat Thermis: ... Atque pedes patriam fulcris petit ille relictis.

s: Fautsch warns that a newcomer who comes to the baths only to indulge his appetite puts his life in danger, because the Genius of the spring is at odds with whoever urges drinking or illicit loves, and ends: do not, with washed feet, pile up filth in your breast.

src.l: Johannes Fautsch, 1618, Schediasma quo duo famosissimi fontes in inferiori Hercyniae sylvae tractu scaturientes ... celebrantur
src.loc: Schediasma, scan p. 7 (end of the poem)
src.q: Qui temere ad Thermas nouus has accesserit hospes, Vt Genio tantum velit indulgere gulæque, Ingenti sese inuoluet discrimine vitæ: Vsque adeò fontis Genius discordat ab ipso, Pocula qui suadet vel iniquæ noctis amores. ... Ne pedibus lotis, cumules in pectore sordes.

src.l: Johannes Fautsch, 1618, Schediasma quo duo famosissimi fontes in inferiori Hercyniae sylvae tractu scaturientes ... celebrantur
src.loc: Schediasma, scan p. 7 (end of the poem)
src.q: Whoever, a new guest, should rashly approach these thermal waters, Wishing only to indulge his own spirit and appetite, Shall involve himself in great danger to his life; So much does the spirit of the spring disagree with one Who encourages drinking bouts or the loves of an unrighteous night. ... lest, with washed feet, you accumulate filth in your heart.
src.qo: Qui temere ad Thermas nouus has accesserit hospes, Vt Genio tantum velit indulgere gulæque, Ingenti sese inuoluet discrimine vitæ: Vsque adeò fontis Genius discordat ab ipso, Pocula qui suadet vel iniquæ noctis amores. ... Ne pedibus lotis, cumules in pectore sordes.

s: In a second poem, on the acidulous springs of the 'Petrina' valley, Fautsch greets 'pious Nymphs, pious powers', 'goddesses who have the keeping of the spring', and asks whether people do not come from everywhere to salute them, sparing no expense, to leave filled with their nectar, rid of disease and with old age delayed.

src.l: Johannes Fautsch, 1618, Schediasma quo duo famosissimi fontes in inferiori Hercyniae sylvae tractu scaturientes ... celebrantur
src.loc: Encomium fontium acidularum vallis Petrinae, scan p. 8
src.q: O igitur saluete piæ, pia Numina Nymphæ, Ter saluete Deæ, quibus est custodia fontis. Nonne salutatum vos gens venit omnis ab omni Latè accita loco, nec parcit sumptibus vllis Nectare dum vestro satiata recedat, et ægris Artubus amoueat morbos seniumque retardet?

src.l: Johannes Fautsch, 1618, Schediasma quo duo famosissimi fontes in inferiori Hercyniae sylvae tractu scaturientes ... celebrantur
src.loc: Encomium fontium acidularum vallis Petrinae, scan p. 8
src.q: O therefore, greetings, pious Nymphs, pious deities, thrice greetings, goddesses, who have the custody of the spring. Does not every person come to greet you, summoned from every place far and wide, nor spare any expense, so long as they depart satisfied with your nectar, and remove diseases from sick limbs and delay old age?
src.qo: O igitur saluete piæ, pia Numina Nymphæ, Ter saluete Deæ, quibus est custodia fontis. Nonne salutatum vos gens venit omnis ab omni Latè accita loco, nec parcit sumptibus vllis Nectare dum vestro satiata recedat, et ægris Artubus amoueat morbos seniumque retardet?

s: Fabian Sommer reports as hearsay ('Fama est') that Emperor Charles IV was hunting where the hot waters now rise when a hound chasing game fell into the boiling marsh and howled, and that the emperor first tried the water on his own body, felt relief, and ordered the place made habitable; Schwenckfeld (1607) dates the story to 1370.

src.l: Fabian Sommer, n.d. (16th c.), De inventione, descriptione, temperie, viribus ... thermarum Caroli IV. libellus
src.loc: De inventione thermarum Caroli IV, scan p. 18 (printed 2)
src.q: Interque venandum canem ardentius feram insecutum, in has, vbi nunc fons ille omnium feruentissimus scaturit, paludes incidisse, et feruore aquae laesum atque excruciatum, clamorem ingentem ex valle ad montes tulisse. ... Imperatorem ipsum primò in proprio corpore huius periculum fecisse, atque leuamen mali (aiunt enim ipsum crus malè affectum habuisse) persensisse, laetatumque felici lauationis successu, locum hunc habitabilem fieri iussisse.

src.l: Caspar Schwenckfeld, 1607, Thermae Teplicenses (Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade)
src.loc: Praefatio, scan p. 30 (printed XI)
src.q: Also ist das CarlesBad von den JagtHunden erstlich erfun den worden. Deßim Jar 1370. als Kayser Carolus Quartus in derselben Gegend auff der Jagt gewesen

src.l: Caspar Schwenckfeld, 1607, Thermae Teplicenses (Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade)
src.loc: Praefatio, scan p. 30 (printed XI)
src.q: Thus, the Carlsbad was first discovered by hunting dogs. In the year 1370, when Emperor Charles IV was in that same region on a hunt
src.qo: Also ist das CarlesBad von den JagtHunden erstlich erfun den worden. Deßim Jar 1370. als Kayser Carolus Quartus in derselben Gegend auff der Jagt gewesen

s: Schwenckfeld tells that the Teplitz bath was revealed by pigs: in 762, when the region was forest and wilderness, herdsmen who had lost some pigs found them on the third day by a warm water whose spring the pigs had laid bare by rooting.

src.l: Caspar Schwenckfeld, 1607, Thermae Teplicenses (Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade)
src.loc: Das Toeplitzer Warme Bad, scan p. 32 (printed 13)
src.q: Anno 762. als dieselbige Gegend / da jekund Töplitz gelegen / lauter Wald vnd Wüsten gewesen ... Vbern dritten Tag finden sie solche wider in einem Walde / bey einem Warmen Wasser / am Quall / welchen sie mit jrem auffwülen entblösset hatten.

src.l: Caspar Schwenckfeld, 1607, Thermae Teplicenses (Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade)
src.loc: Das Toeplitzer Warme Bad, scan p. 32 (printed 13)
src.q: In the year 762, when the same region where Teplitz now lies was nothing but forest and wilderness ... On the third day, they found them again in a forest, by a warm spring, which they had exposed by their rooting.
src.qo: Anno 762. als dieselbige Gegend / da jekund Töplitz gelegen / lauter Wald vnd Wüsten gewesen ... Vbern dritten Tag finden sie solche wider in einem Walde / bey einem Warmen Wasser / am Quall / welchen sie mit jrem auffwülen entblösset hatten.

s: Schwenckfeld says tests and experience show the Teplitz warm water carries a rock salt, coal, a sulphurous pyrites and a little limestone, and that frogs have been heard croaking in it at Christmas in the hardest winter.

src.l: Caspar Schwenckfeld, 1607, Thermae Teplicenses (Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade)
src.loc: Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade, scan p. 45 (printed 26)
src.q: Was dieses Warmen Wassers Halt anreichet, geben die Proben neben dem Effect und Erfahrung, daß es führe ein Bergsalk, SteinKolen, sampt einem Schwefelichten Kyß und wenig Kalckstein. ... Im härtesten und kältesten Winter umb Weyhnachten, hat man etlich mal die Frösche darinnen hören quarren und schreyen.

src.l: Caspar Schwenckfeld, 1607, Thermae Teplicenses (Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade)
src.loc: Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade, scan p. 45 (printed 26)
src.q: Regarding the composition of this warm water, the tests, along with the effect and experience, indicate that it contains mountain salt, coal, together with a sulfurous pyrites and a little limestone. ... In the hardest and coldest winter around Christmas, one has several times heard frogs croaking and crying in it.
src.qo: Was dieses Warmen Wassers Halt anreichet, geben die Proben neben dem Effect und Erfahrung, daß es führe ein Bergsalk, SteinKolen, sampt einem Schwefelichten Kyß und wenig Kalckstein. ... Im härtesten und kältesten Winter umb Weyhnachten, hat man etlich mal die Frösche darinnen hören quarren und schreyen.

s: Schwenckfeld says he chose to annex his short account of the warm bath at Teplitz to 'the Hirschberg warm bath' so that patients could compare the two baths, and refers readers who want rules for eating, drinking and conduct in the bath to the little treatise he wrote on the Hirschberg warm bath.

src.l: Caspar Schwenckfeld, 1607, Thermae Teplicenses (Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade)
src.loc: Dedicatoria, scan p. 16 (sig. a v)
src.q: ein kurtz doch gründlich Verzeichniß deß weitberühm- ten vnd vortrefflichen Warmen Bades/ welches zu Töplitz in Böhmen gelegen/ dem Hirsch- bergischen Warmen Bade an- nectiren wollen

src.l: Caspar Schwenckfeld, 1607, Thermae Teplicenses (Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade)
src.loc: Dedicatoria, scan p. 16 (sig. a v)
src.q: compiled a short yet thorough record of the far-famed and excellent Warm Bath, which is located in Teplitz in Bohemia, I have chosen to annex it to the Hirschberg Warm Bath
src.qo: ein kurtz doch gründlich Verzeichniß deß weitberühm- ten vnd vortrefflichen Warmen Bades/ welches zu Töplitz in Böhmen gelegen/ dem Hirsch- bergischen Warmen Bade an- nectiren wollen

src.l: Caspar Schwenckfeld, 1607, Thermae Teplicenses (Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade)
src.loc: Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade, scan p. 51 (printed 32)
src.q: Wer davon weitleufftigern Bericht wil haben / wessen er sich im Bade mit Essen / Trincken / vnd dergleichen verhalten solle / besehe das Tractätlin / welches ich vom Hirschbergischen Warmen Bade / allen den jenigen / welche sich der Warmen Bäder gebrauchen wollen / zum Unterricht vnnd Wolgefallen geschrieben habe.

src.l: Caspar Schwenckfeld, 1607, Thermae Teplicenses (Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade)
src.loc: Von dem Toeplitzer Warmen Bade, scan p. 51 (printed 32)
src.q: Whoever wishes to have a more detailed report on how he should conduct himself in the bath with eating, drinking, and the like, should look at the little treatise which I have written for the instruction and pleasure of all those who wish to use the warm baths, concerning the Hirschbergischen Warmen Bade.
src.qo: Wer davon weitleufftigern Bericht wil haben / wessen er sich im Bade mit Essen / Trincken / vnd dergleichen verhalten solle / besehe das Tractätlin / welches ich vom Hirschbergischen Warmen Bade / allen den jenigen / welche sich der Warmen Bäder gebrauchen wollen / zum Unterricht vnnd Wolgefallen geschrieben habe.

s: Paracelsus grants that there is much fire in the earth and that water veins running through it come out warm, but denies that the water of Pfäfers arises so, because it shows no taste or admixture of that earthly firing as many other baths do: it is a pure clear water with no taste.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Buecher und Schrifften, parts 7-10 (ed. Huser): Von dem Bad Pfeffers
src.loc: Von dem Bad Pfeffers, scan p. 350 (printed 331)
src.q: daz auch in der Erden solches Fewrs viel seye / und die Wasseradern / so dardurch lauffend / von ihnen gewärmet werden ... Das aber dieses Wasser also sein ursprung neme / soll widerredt werden ... Dann es an jhm selbst ein lautter klar Wasser / das keim Corpus anhenckt / auch keinerley Geschmack erfunden wird.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Buecher und Schrifften, parts 7-10 (ed. Huser): Von dem Bad Pfeffers
src.loc: Von dem Bad Pfeffers, scan p. 350 (printed 331)
src.q: there is much of such fire in the earth, and the water veins that run through it are warmed by them ... However, it should be disputed that this water takes its origin in this way ... for it is in itself a pure, clear water that adheres to no body, nor is any taste found in it.
src.qo: daz auch in der Erden solches Fewrs viel seye / und die Wasseradern / so dardurch lauffend / von ihnen gewärmet werden ... Das aber dieses Wasser also sein ursprung neme / soll widerredt werden ... Dann es an jhm selbst ein lautter klar Wasser / das keim Corpus anhenckt / auch keinerley Geschmack erfunden wird.

s: Paracelsus says the bath of Pfäfers renews itself yearly: its rejuvenation begins in spring and ends in winter, it grows with the herbs and dies with them, forced out by the power of the sun as the herbs are.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Buecher und Schrifften, parts 7-10 (ed. Huser): Von dem Bad Pfeffers
src.loc: Von dem Bad Pfeffers, scan p. 351 (printed 332)
src.q: Also merckend auch von dem Bad Pfeffers/ das sein veriüngerung angeht im Früling/ vnd terminiert sich im Winter/ wachset mit den Kreuttern/ stirbt mit jhnen.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Buecher und Schrifften, parts 7-10 (ed. Huser): Von dem Bad Pfeffers
src.loc: Von dem Bad Pfeffers, scan p. 351 (printed 332)
src.q: Thus, note also of the Bath at Pfeffers that its rejuvenation begins in the spring and terminates in the winter, growing with the herbs and dying with them.
src.qo: Also merckend auch von dem Bad Pfeffers/ das sein veriüngerung angeht im Früling/ vnd terminiert sich im Winter/ wachset mit den Kreuttern/ stirbt mit jhnen.

s: Paracelsus says of Pfäfers that matter shut in the body which cannot leave by the sweat-pores must come out through the skin itself, 'so mighty is the power of this bath', and that the bath is its own digestive and syrup.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Buecher und Schrifften, parts 1-10 (ed. Huser): Von dem Bad Pfeffers
src.loc: Von dem Bad Pfeffers, scan p. 2487 (printed 336)
src.q: so muß die Haut hinweg/ auff daß herauß komme. So gewaltig ist die Krafft diß Bads. ... das Bad ist sein eigen Digestiuum vnd Syrup/ was es in mitler zeit zeitig macht/ lasset es auch außziehen.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Buecher und Schrifften, parts 1-10 (ed. Huser): Von dem Bad Pfeffers
src.loc: Von dem Bad Pfeffers, scan p. 2487 (printed 336)
src.q: the skin must be removed so that it may come out. Such is the power of this bath. ... the bath is its own digestivum and syrup; what it makes ready in the meantime, it also lets be drawn out.
src.qo: so muß die Haut hinweg/ auff daß herauß komme. So gewaltig ist die Krafft diß Bads. ... das Bad ist sein eigen Digestiuum vnd Syrup/ was es in mitler zeit zeitig macht/ lasset es auch außziehen.

s: Kolweck (1631) reports that before the bridge was built one could reach the bath of Pfäfers only by a very long rope or hanging ladder, that fright and dizziness spoiled the bath for many who saw the steep way down, and that others had themselves let down by their servants tied in chairs with covered eyes, or carried on shoulders.

src.l: Johann Kolweck, 1631, Tractat von dess ueberauss heylsamen ... Vnser Lieben Frawen Pfefersbad
src.loc: Cap. III, scan p. 71 (printed 59)
src.q: hat man/ ohne Mittel/ eines sehr langen Sails oder Stricks / entweders obhangender Lait= ter/ keines Weegs / zu dem Bad / vnnd ohne grosse Gefahr / nicht kommen kön= nen

src.l: Johann Kolweck, 1631, Tractat von dess ueberauss heylsamen ... Vnser Lieben Frawen Pfefersbad
src.loc: Cap. III, scan p. 72 (printed 60)
src.q: ist jhnen auß Schrecken vnnd Schwindel/ das Bad erleydet ... Zwar haben sich andere/in Seßlen angehefft mit verdeckten Augen / durch jhre Diener / hinab lenden/ andere auff den Achßlen/vnd Schultern hinab tra= gen lassen

s: Montaigne says he has seen nearly all the famous baths of Christendom and for some years has used them, that he holds bathing healthy in general, and believes we suffer no small harm to health from having lost the custom of washing the body every day.

src.l: Michel de Montaigne, 1598, Les Essais (Paris 1598)
src.loc: Essais II.37, scan p. 816 (printed 798)
src.q: I'ay veu par occasion de mes voyages, quasi tous les bains fameux de Chrestienté, & depuis quel- ques annees ay commencé à m'en seruir: Car en general i'e- stime le baigner salubre ... croy que nous encourons non legeres incommoditez, en nostre santé, pour auoir perdu cette coustume ... de se lauer le corps tous les iours

src.l: Michel de Montaigne, 1598, Les Essais (Paris 1598)
src.loc: Essais II.37, scan p. 816 (printed 798)
src.q: I have seen, by way of my travels, nearly all the famous baths of Christendom, and for some years have begun to make use of them: For in general I consider bathing wholesome, and believe that we incur no slight inconveniences to our health for having lost this custom ... of washing the body every day
src.qo: I'ay veu par occasion de mes voyages, quasi tous les bains fameux de Chrestienté, & depuis quel- ques annees ay commencé à m'en seruir: Car en general i'e- stime le baigner salubre ... croy que nous encourons non legeres incommoditez, en nostre santé, pour auoir perdu cette coustume ... de se lauer le corps tous les iours

s: Montaigne says whoever does not bring enough cheerfulness to enjoy the company found at the baths and the walks the beauty of the places invites loses the best and surest part of their effect, and that he therefore chose baths with the most pleasant site, lodging, food and company.

src.l: Michel de Montaigne, 1598, Les Essais (Paris 1598)
src.loc: Essais II.37, scan p. 817 (printed 799)
src.q: Qui n'y apporte assez d'allegresse, pour pouuoir iouyr le plaisir des compagnies qui s'y trouuent, & des promenades & exercices, à quoy nous conuie la beauté des lieux, où sont communement assises ces eaux, il perd sans doubte la meilleure piece & plus asseuree de leur effect

src.l: Michel de Montaigne, 1598, Les Essais (Paris 1598)
src.loc: Essais II.37, scan p. 817 (printed 799)
src.q: He who does not bring enough cheer there to be able to enjoy the pleasure of the companies who are found there, and of the walks and exercises to which we are invited by the beauty of the places where these waters are commonly situated, loses without doubt the best and most assured part of their effect.
src.qo: Qui n'y apporte assez d'allegresse, pour pouuoir iouyr le plaisir des compagnies qui s'y trouuent, & des promenades & exercices, à quoy nous conuie la beauté des lieux, où sont communement assises ces eaux, il perd sans doubte la meilleure piece & plus asseuree de leur effect

s: Montaigne says he perceived no extraordinary or miraculous effect at the baths and, on enquiring more closely than is usual, found the rumours of such workings ill-founded and false; but he saw hardly anyone the waters made worse.

src.l: Michel de Montaigne, 1598, Les Essais (Paris 1598)
src.loc: Essais II.37, scan p. 817 (printed 799)
src.q: Et encores que ie n'y aye apperceu aucun effect extraordinaire & miraculeux ... i'aye trouué mal fondez & faux, tous les bruits de telles operations, qui se sement en ces lieux là ... Toutesfois aussi n'ay-ie veu guere de personnes que ces eaux ayent empiré

src.l: Michel de Montaigne, 1598, Les Essais (Paris 1598)
src.loc: Essais II.37, scan p. 817 (printed 799)
src.q: And although I have not perceived any extraordinary and miraculous effect ... I have found all the rumors of such operations, which are sown in those places and believed there (as the world easily deceives itself with what it desires), to be ill-founded and false ... Nevertheless, I have also seen hardly any persons whom these waters have made worse
src.qo: Et encores que ie n'y aye apperceu aucun effect extraordinaire & miraculeux ... i'aye trouué mal fondez & faux, tous les bruits de telles operations, qui se sement en ces lieux là ... Toutesfois aussi n'ay-ie veu guere de personnes que ces eaux ayent empiré

s: Mercuriale concludes from Juvenal, Martial, Clement of Alexandria, Cyprian and Jerome that the custom of men and women washing in mixed baths lasted a long time at Rome and elsewhere, and reports (from Dio Cassius) that Hadrian wanted men bathed apart from women.

src.l: Girolamo Mercuriale, 1672, De arte gymnastica libri sex (Amsterdam 1672)
src.loc: De arte gymnastica I, scan p. 77 (printed 57)
src.q: His itaque omnibus cuivis perspectum esse potest, non pauco tempore eum morem & Romae, & alibi perdurasse; ut foeminae atque viri in promiscuis balneis lavarentur ... qualis fuit Hadrianus princeps, quem scribit Dion Cassius viros discretos à foeminis lavari voluisse

src.l: Girolamo Mercuriale, 1672, De arte gymnastica libri sex (Amsterdam 1672)
src.loc: De arte gymnastica I, scan p. 77 (printed 57)
src.q: Thus, from all these, it can be clear to anyone that this custom lasted for no short time, both at Rome and elsewhere, that women and men were bathed in promiscuous baths ... Such was the prince Hadrian, whom Dion Cassius writes wished for men to be bathed separately from women
src.qo: His itaque omnibus cuivis perspectum esse potest, non pauco tempore eum morem & Romae, & alibi perdurasse; ut foeminae atque viri in promiscuis balneis lavarentur ... qualis fuit Hadrianus princeps, quem scribit Dion Cassius viros discretos à foeminis lavari voluisse

s: Schroeter's astrological tables (1551) have a table 'at what time a fitting bath should be chosen': the earthy signs and Gemini are bad, seven signs are good, the Moon's aspects with Jupiter and Venus help, and her conjunction, opposition or square with Saturn and Mars hinder.

src.l: Johannes von Schroeter, 1551, Tabulae ex quibus quisque facile discet, qua via praedictiones rerum futurarum elici debeant
src.loc: Tabulae, scan p. 15
src.q: Quo tempore conueniens balneum eligi debeat. Signa terrea et ♊, mala. Bona { ♈, ♌, ♎, ♒, ♐, ♓, ♋ } Aspectus promouentes. ☽ in { ☌, ⚹, □, △ } cum ♃ et ♀. ☽ in { ⚹, △ } ♄ ♂ ☉, non impeditur. Aspectus impedientes. ☽ in { ☌, ☍, □ } ♄ et ♂.

s: Brunschwig (1512) describes a 'Balneum marie' built in a bathing tub: a copper pipe holding the coals passes through the tub's floor, the water stands round the pipe, and the cucurbits with their alembics are set in that water; he calls it the best furnace of all.

src.l: Hieronymus Brunschwig, 1512, Das Buch zu distillieren (Strassburg 1512)
src.loc: Das erste Buch, scan p. 117
src.q: Dar nach soltu haben ein ander Balneum marie. in einer bad bütten ... vnd in die rör geworffen würt kolen/vnnd das wasser vßer vmb die rör / dar in das feuer ist/vnd in das selbig wasser zü ring vmb werden gesetzt die cucurbit mit dem alembic. ... vnd das ist der aller best öfen genant Balneum marie in einer bad bütten.

s: A lexicon entry under Ruland's running head defines 'Balneum Mariae, or maris as many would have it called' as a distilling furnace holding water in which, when hot, the chemical vessels are set for the putrefaction of their matter and for separation.

src.l: Martin Ruland, 1668, Lexicon page (running head 'Rulandi phil. et medici') in the SL volume catalogued as Borch, De ortu et progressu chemiae (1668)
src.loc: Lexicon s.v. Balneum Mariae, scan p. 359 (printed 99)
src.q: Balneum Mariæ, vel maris, vt multi vocari volunt, est furnus destillatorius, aqua continens, in qua calente vasa chymica ponuntur ad putrefactionem suæ materiæ, quam capiunt, ad separationem, et id genus humidarum ascensionum perficiendas operationes.

src.l: Martin Ruland, 1668, Lexicon page (running head 'Rulandi phil. et medici') in the SL volume catalogued as Borch, De ortu et progressu chemiae (1668)
src.loc: Lexicon s.v. Balneum Mariae, scan p. 359 (printed 99)
src.q: Bath of Mary, or bath of the sea, as many wish it to be called, is a distilling furnace containing water, in which, when heated, chemical vessels are placed for the putrefaction of their matter which they contain, for separation, and for performing operations of that kind of moist ascensions.
src.qo: Balneum Mariæ, vel maris, vt multi vocari volunt, est furnus destillatorius, aqua continens, in qua calente vasa chymica ponuntur ad putrefactionem suæ materiæ, quam capiunt, ad separationem, et id genus humidarum ascensionum perficiendas operationes.

s: The Rosarium philosophorum says the fire of dung is the active cause in the digestion of 'our stone', and that the fire of the bath of Mary, though very temperate, will not serve in its place.

src.l: Anonymous (Rosarium philosophorum; Clangor buccinae), ed. Guglielmo Grataroli, 1572, Auriferae artis, quam chemiam vocant (Basel 1572)
src.loc: Rosarium philosophorum, scan p. 984 (printed 242)
src.q: Ignis fimi est causa agens in opere digestionis lapidis nostri, nec valet ignis balnei Mariæ, quamvis etiam temperatissimus sit, loco illius.

src.l: Anonymous (Rosarium philosophorum; Clangor buccinae), ed. Guglielmo Grataroli, 1572, Auriferae artis, quam chemiam vocant (Basel 1572)
src.loc: Rosarium philosophorum, scan p. 984 (printed 242)
src.q: The fire of dung is the active cause in the work of digestion of our stone; nor is the fire of the bath of Mary of any use in its place
src.qo: Ignis fimi est causa agens in opere digestionis lapidis nostri, nec valet ignis balnei Mariæ, quamvis etiam temperatissimus sit, loco illius.

s: In the Rosarium philosophorum the stage headed 'Ablutio vel mundificatio' carries the German couplet: here the dew falls from heaven and washes the black body in the grave.

src.loc: Rosarium philosophorum, scan p. 1035 (printed 303)
src.q: ABLVTIO VEL mundificatio Hie felt der Tanw von himmel herab/ Vnd wascht den schwartzen leyb im grab ab.

src.q: ABLUTION OR purification Here the dew falls down from heaven, And washes the black body in the grave.

s: The tract Clangor buccinae says 'our copper' has a dropsical body as Naaman the Syrian had a leprous one, and so seeks the 'lavacrum regenerationis' seven times in the Jordan to be cleansed of its inborn passions and corruptions.

src.l: Anonymous (Rosarium philosophorum; Clangor buccinae), ed. Guglielmo Grataroli, 1572, Auriferae artis, quam chemiam vocant (Basel 1572)
src.loc: Clangor buccinae, scan p. 559 (printed 537)
src.q: Æs nostrum corpus habet hydropicum, vt Naaman Syrus leprosum, propter quod quærit lauacrum regenerationis septies in Iordane, vt ab innatis passionibus & corruptionib. emundetur.

src.l: Anonymous (Rosarium philosophorum; Clangor buccinae), ed. Guglielmo Grataroli, 1572, Auriferae artis, quam chemiam vocant (Basel 1572)
src.loc: Clangor buccinae, scan p. 559 (printed 537)
src.q: Our copper has a dropsical body, as Naaman the Syrian had a leprous one, on account of which it seeks the bath of regeneration seven times in the Jordan, so that it may be cleansed from inborn passions and corruptions.
src.qo: Æs nostrum corpus habet hydropicum, vt Naaman Syrus leprosum, propter quod quærit lauacrum regenerationis septies in Iordane, vt ab innatis passionibus & corruptionib. emundetur.

s: Splendor solis, in its seventh parable, cites 'Ovid the old poet' for an old man who wished to be made young again: he should have himself cut in pieces and boiled until fully cooked and no further, and then the limbs would reunite and grow young in great strength.

src.l: Salomon Trismosin (attrib.), 1598, Aureum vellus oder Guldin Schatz und Kunstkammer (Rorschach 1598): Splendor solis
src.loc: Splendor solis, Die Sibendte Gleichnus, scan p. 263 (printed 29)
src.q: Ovidius der Alt Poet hat dergleichen angezeigt / so er schreibt vonn der weissen alten / der sich widerumb wolte verjüngern / er solte sich lassen zertheylen / vnnd kochen / biß zu seiner vollkommnen kochung / vnd nicht weiter / dann wurden sich die Glieder wider Vereinigen / vnnd widerumb verjüngen in vil Kräfften.

src.l: Salomon Trismosin (attrib.), 1598, Aureum vellus oder Guldin Schatz und Kunstkammer (Rorschach 1598): Splendor solis
src.loc: Splendor solis, Die Sibendte Gleichnus, scan p. 263 (printed 29)
src.q: Ovid, the old poet, has indicated something similar when he writes of the white old man who wanted to rejuvenate himself again; he was to have himself divided and cooked until his perfect cooking, and no further, then the limbs would unite again and rejuvenate in many powers.
src.qo: Ovidius der Alt Poet hat dergleichen angezeigt / so er schreibt vonn der weissen alten / der sich widerumb wolte verjüngern / er solte sich lassen zertheylen / vnnd kochen / biß zu seiner vollkommnen kochung / vnd nicht weiter / dann wurden sich die Glieder wider Vereinigen / vnnd widerumb verjüngen in vil Kräfften.

s: Stoltzius' epigram on the second key of Basil Valentine has Sol and Diana lay their clothes aside and be naked for the bridal bed, and a precious water drawn from two fighters in which the bride washes her body for the groom.

src.l: Daniel Stoltzius von Stoltzenberg, 1624, Viridarium chymicum figuris cupro incisis adornatum (Frankfurt 1624)
src.loc: Viridarium chymicum, Secunda clavis Basilii, scan p. 24
src.q: Vestibus abjectis, Sol nudus & ipsa Diana Nuda sit, optatus manet ut inde torus. Sponsæ ex athletis pretiosa sit unda duobus, Pro Sponso proprium corpus ut illa lavet.

src.l: Daniel Stoltzius von Stoltzenberg, 1624, Viridarium chymicum figuris cupro incisis adornatum (Frankfurt 1624)
src.loc: Viridarium chymicum, Secunda clavis Basilii, scan p. 24
src.q: With garments cast aside, let the Sun be naked, and Diana herself Be naked, so that the desired bridal chamber may remain from it. Let there be precious water from the two athletes for the bride, So that she may wash her own body for the sake of the groom.
src.qo: Vestibus abjectis, Sol nudus & ipsa Diana Nuda sit, optatus manet ut inde torus. Sponsæ ex athletis pretiosa sit unda duobus, Pro Sponso proprium corpus ut illa lavet.

s: Peter Martyr reports that explorers tell of an island named Boiuca or Agnameo, 325 leagues from Hispaniola, with a perennial spring whose water, drunk, makes old men young again; asked his own view, he says he does not grant nature so much and thinks God has kept this prerogative for himself.

src.l: Petrus Martyr Anglerius (Peter Martyr d'Anghiera), 1533, De rebus oceanicis et orbe novo decades (Basel 1533)
src.loc: Decade II, book 10, scan p. 113 (printed f. 42)
src.q: una esse insulam fabulantur, qui eam explorarunt ad intima, nomine Boiuca, alias Agnameo, fonte perenni adeo nobilem, ut eius fontis aqua epota senes reiuuenescant. ... Ego uero si quid sentiam interrogaueris: naturae rerum genitrici non me tantum tribuere respondebo, sibique seruasse deum hanc praerogatiuam

src.l: Petrus Martyr Anglerius (Peter Martyr d'Anghiera), 1533, De rebus oceanicis et orbe novo decades (Basel 1533)
src.loc: Decade II, book 10, scan p. 113 (printed f. 42)
src.q: they tell a fable of one island three hundred and twenty-five leagues from Hispaniola ... so noble for its perennial fountain that the water of that spring, when drunk, makes the elderly grow young again. ... I will answer that I do not attribute so much to Nature, the mother of things, and I believe that God has reserved for Himself this prerogative
src.qo: una esse insulam fabulantur, qui eam explorarunt ad intima, nomine Boiuca, alias Agnameo, fonte perenni adeo nobilem, ut eius fontis aqua epota senes reiuuenescant. ... Ego uero si quid sentiam interrogaueris: naturae rerum genitrici non me tantum tribuere respondebo, sibique seruasse deum hanc praerogatiuam

s: A German alchemical tract of about 1700 says Peter Martyr 'assures' in his Decades that on the island 'Bonique' there is a spring from which old people who drink become young and strong again, though the hair stays grey and the wrinkles remain, and that such waters were therefore called springs of youth.

src.l: Anonymous, 1700, Communication einer vortrefflichen Chymischen Medicin (c. 1700)
src.loc: Communication einer vortrefflichen Chymischen Medicin, scan p. 47
src.q: Petrus Martyr Augerius, ein Meyländer / versi- chert in seinen Decadibus, daß in der In- sul Bonique ein Brunnen sey / wovon wann die alte Leute trincken / sie wieder jung und starck werden / obwolen die Haa- re grau bleiben / und die Kuntzeln im Ge- sichte nicht vergehen ... welche dahero Brunnen der Ju- gend sind genannt worden.

src.l: Anonymous, 1700, Communication einer vortrefflichen Chymischen Medicin (c. 1700)
src.loc: Communication einer vortrefflichen Chymischen Medicin, scan p. 47
src.q: Petrus Martyr Augerius, a Milanese, assures in his Decadibus that on the island of Bonique there is a fountain from which, when old people drink, they become young and strong again, although the hair remains gray and the wrinkles in the face do not disappear ... which were therefore called Brunnen der Jugend
src.qo: Petrus Martyr Augerius, ein Meyländer / versi- chert in seinen Decadibus, daß in der In- sul Bonique ein Brunnen sey / wovon wann die alte Leute trincken / sie wieder jung und starck werden / obwolen die Haa- re grau bleiben / und die Kuntzeln im Ge- sichte nicht vergehen ... welche dahero Brunnen der Ju- gend sind genannt worden.

s: Seneca opens Ep. 56 by saying that a varied clamour sounds all round him because he lodges directly above a bath (balneum).

src.l: Seneca, 1827, L. Annaei Senecae opera philosophica, vol. 3 (ed. Bouillet)
src.loc: Ep. 56.1, scan p. 351
src.q: Ecce varius clamor undique me circumsonat; supra ipsum balneum habito

src.l: Seneca, 1827, L. Annaei Senecae opera philosophica, vol. 3 (ed. Bouillet)
src.loc: Ep. 56.1, scan p. 351
src.q: Behold, a varied clamor resounds around me from all sides; I live above the bath itself.
src.qo: Ecce varius clamor undique me circumsonat; supra ipsum balneum habito

s: Among the noises Seneca (Ep. 56) hears from the bath below are the slap of a hand on shoulders, changing with a flat or cupped palm, and people leaping into the pool (piscina) with a great splash.

src.l: Seneca, 1827, L. Annaei Senecae opera philosophica, vol. 3 (ed. Bouillet)
src.q: audio crepitum illisæ manus humeris; quæ, prout plana pervenit, aut concava, ita sonum mutat.

s: Seneca (Ep. 86) says that baths were once few and unadorned, because a thing costing a quadrans was devised for use and not for delight.

s: Seneca (Ep. 86) says it mattered little to Scipio that his bath water was often cloudy, because he came there to wash off sweat, not unguent.

src.qo: Nec multum ejus intererat, an sic lavaretur; veniebat enim, ut sudorem illic ablueret, non ut unguentum.

s: Oczko says he wrote the book to describe what the cieplice are good for and how to use them, astonished that so many people, some of them of standing, use these springs on one another's say-so, like the blind riding after the blind, and still do not know when to begin, how to use them, or when to stop.

s: Bacci says 'Holy Water' (Aqua Sancta) is a common surname of many baths, especially in Italy, and that baths named for saints carry the saint's cure: Saint George's heals wounds, Saint Lucy's the eyes, Saint Bartholomew's diseases of the skin.

s: Bacci says the pagans of Rome had a Water of Mercury before the Latin Gate which, sprinkled over the people, was thought to wash away crimes and clear them of perjury, and that the place was dedicated to Saint John the Baptist to remove the superstition.

s: Bacci reports from Valerius Maximus that among the old Romans a father did not bathe with his grown son nor a father-in-law with his sons-in-law, because it was thought wrong to strip among those sacred bonds, as in a consecrated place; and from Plutarch that Cato the Censor was praised for never bathing with his son.

s: Bacci judges that, for all the nakedness of the Roman baths, women's modesty lasted a very long time and they did not enter the baths together with men except through abuse; hence, he says, the many private baths and some public baths for women.

s: In Panteo's dialogue on the Caldiero springs (1553 De balneis), asked whether the ancients allowed baths only for health, the speaker Aleardus answers yes, but that from health everyone slid into a very soft licence in bathing, nobles and commoners frequenting the daily bath beyond custom.

s: Puzzled by Vitruvius's sloping hypocaust floor on which a ball thrown in rolls back to the furnace mouth, Pantheus conjectures that a slave threw balls into the furnace to stir the dying flames, and reads Seneca's ball-counter and Statius's floors 'that will hear the rattling balls' as support.

s: After Pantheus explains that the baptisteria of Roman baths were tubs of wood or marble for immersion, named from Greek baptizein 'to immerse', Aleardus concludes that the baptistery of Christian churches, where infants are cleansed by threefold immersion, takes its name from the bath's; Pantheus agrees.

s: In Panteo's dialogue, Hermolaus cites the probatic pool at Jerusalem, with five porches, where the blind, lame and withered who plunged in when the waters were stirred by divine power returned to health, as Scripture's witness that 'piscina' could mean a bathing pool.

s: Aleardo Pedemonte, physician of Verona, lists among the powers of the Caldiero baths that, taken every year for at least fifteen days with the rules observed, they keep a man in youthfulness.

s: Aleardo's rules for drinking the Caldiero water: go at dawn and drink at the spring, because water carried half a mile loses half its power; and do not take it at the conjunction or opposition of the moon, when it is pestilential.

s: At Plombières the locals found Montaigne's way strange: without any prior medicine he drank nine glasses of the water, about a pot, every morning at seven.

s: The journal describes the principal bath at Plombières as an oval of ancient construction, thirty-five paces by fifteen, where hot water wells up from below through several springs and cold water is let in from above to temper it as the bathers wish.

s: The journal says a singular modesty is observed in the Plombières bath, and it is indecent for men to bathe other than naked except for small breeches, and for women except for a shift.

s: The journal copies the ordinance of the bailiff of the Vosges, renewed yearly on a board before the great bath in German and French, which forbids prostitutes and immodest women to enter the baths or come within five hundred paces of them, on pain of the whip at the four corners of the baths, and punishes innkeepers who harbour them with prison and a fine.

s: At Baden the journal says the inn where they lodged had once fed three hundred mouths in a day, still had a large company with some hundred and seventy beds in use.
