s: Leo Africanus (in the 1632 Latin version) says Fez has more than a hundred baths of elegant build, unequal in size but all made on the same plan, each with four halls; the next page (scan 292) adds raised walkways outside, up five or six steps, where men undress and go naked to the bath.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, 'Balnea', printed p. 288, scan p. 291 (continues on scan p. 292)
src.q: Reperias præterea in hac urbe plusquam centum balnea, multo artificio atque ſtructura elegantiſſima: & quamvis inæqualis ſint magnitudinis, omnia tamen ad eundem modum ſunt fabricata.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, 'Balnea', printed p. 288, scan p. 291 (continues on scan p. 292)
src.q: You may also find in this city more than one hundred baths, of much artifice and very elegant structure; and although they are of unequal size, they are all built in the same manner.
src.qo: Reperias præterea in hac urbe plusquam centum balnea, multo artificio atque ſtructura elegantiſſima: & quamvis inæqualis ſint magnitudinis, omnia tamen ad eundem modum ſunt fabricata.

s: Leo describes the route through a Fez bath: first a cold hall where cold water is kept to temper the hot, then a warmer room where servants clean and wash the bathers, then the third room, the steam room, where one sweats as long as one likes.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 289, scan p. 292
src.q: Primò igitur balneum intrare volentes, aulam quandam transeunt frigidam, in qua frigida servatur aqua, qua calidam cōmiscere solent, deinde ad alium locum aliquanto calidiorem itur, ubi à servis mundantur atque abluuntur: postea ad tertium vaporarium, ubi quantùm lubet sudatur

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 289, scan p. 292
src.q: those wishing to enter the bath first pass through a cold hall, in which cold water is kept, with which they are accustomed to mix the hot; then they go to another place somewhat warmer, where they are cleaned and washed by servants; afterwards, they proceed to the third steam room, where they may sweat as much as they please.
src.qo: Primò igitur balneum intrare volentes, aulam quandam transeunt frigidam, in qua frigida servatur aqua, qua calidam cōmiscere solent, deinde ad alium locum aliquanto calidiorem itur, ubi à servis mundantur atque abluuntur: postea ad tertium vaporarium, ubi quantùm lubet sudatur

s: In the Fez steam room the water is heated in a boiler; each bather is given two wooden vessels of it, and whoever wants more pays the attendant extra, while the master of the steam room takes only two small coins.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 289, scan p. 292
src.q: Cuique homini ejus aquæ duo dantur vasa, qui plura, aut qui largius lavari volunt, ministro ad minimum liardum exsolvunt, vaporarii autem domino duo tantùm teruncii numerantur.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 289, scan p. 292
src.q: For every man, two vessels of this water are given; those who want more, or who wish to wash more lavishly, pay the attendant at least a liard, and to the master of the steam room, only two teruncii are paid.
src.qo: Cuique homini ejus aquæ duo dantur vasa, qui plura, aut qui largius lavari volunt, ministro ad minimum liardum exsolvunt, vaporarii autem domino duo tantùm teruncii numerantur.

s: Leo says the Fez baths heat their water only with dried animal dung, which many boys gather from the stables into heaps outside the town and leave two or three months in the sun before burning.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 289, scan p. 292
src.q: Ignis quo aqua calefit non nisi stercore quorundam animalium desiccato exstruitur: quamobrem permulti ad hoc aluntur pueri, qui huc atque illuc per stabula discurrentes, stercus omne extra oppidum in cumulum congerunt

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 289, scan p. 292
src.q: The fire by which the water is heated is constructed with nothing but the dried dung of certain animals
src.qo: Ignis quo aqua calefit non nisi stercore quorundam animalium desiccato exstruitur: quamobrem permulti ad hoc aluntur pueri, qui huc atque illuc per stabula discurrentes, stercus omne extra oppidum in cumulum congerunt

s: Women in Fez have their own steam rooms; baths shared by both sexes open to men from the third to the fourteenth hour and to women the rest of the day, and while women bathe a rope is stretched across the first entrance to tell men not to go further.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 290, scan p. 293 (sentence begins on scan p. 292)
src.q: viris nempe à tertia uſque in decimamquartam diei horam, reliquum temporis mulieribus patent. Interea dum ſe fœminæ abluunt, funem in primum ingreſſum extendunt, qui viros tum temporis non ulterius introeundum eſſe indicat.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 290, scan p. 293 (sentence begins on scan p. 292)
src.q: namely, they are open to men from the third until the fourteenth hour of the day, and for the rest of the time to the women. Meanwhile, while the women are washing themselves, they stretch a rope across the first entrance, which indicates to the men that they are not to enter further at that time.
src.qo: viris nempe à tertia uſque in decimamquartam diei horam, reliquum temporis mulieribus patent. Interea dum ſe fœminæ abluunt, funem in primum ingreſſum extendunt, qui viros tum temporis non ulterius introeundum eſſe indicat.

s: Leo says bathers in Fez sing loudly after washing; youths go naked while men cover themselves with a small cloth; the bather is laid on the ground, anointed and scraped with instruments, and the rich are given a cloth to lie on and a wooden pillow.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 290, scan p. 293
src.q: Solent hic tam viri quàm fœminæ genio admodum indulgere poſt lotionem atq; cantiunculis vocaliſſimis animi lætitiam indicare. Iuvenes nudi fine aliquo pudore balneum intrant, viri autem pudenda linteolo tegunt. … Ditioribus pannum feretrum ſubſternere ſolent, caput verò in ligneum pulvinar panno feretro tectum reclinare jubent.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 290, scan p. 293
src.q: Both men and women are accustomed to indulge their spirits here after washing and to show the joy of their hearts with very vocal singing. Youths enter the bath naked without any shame, but men cover their private parts with a small cloth.
src.qo: Solent hic tam viri quàm fœminæ genio admodum indulgere poſt lotionem atq; cantiunculis vocaliſſimis animi lætitiam indicare. Iuvenes nudi fine aliquo pudore balneum intrant, viri autem pudenda linteolo tegunt. … Ditioribus pannum feretrum ſubſternere ſolent, caput verò in ligneum pulvinar panno feretro tectum reclinare jubent.

s: Barbers and surgeons work in the Fez baths, and most baths belong to mosques and colleges, paying them large sums every year.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 290, scan p. 293
src.q: Reperias quoque hic tonſores atq; chirurgos complures, qui & hic officium exercent ſuum. Maxima balneorum pars ad templa atq; collegia pertinent

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 290, scan p. 293
src.q: You may also find here many barbers and surgeons, who also ply their trade here. The greatest part of the baths belong to temples and colleges
src.qo: Reperias quoque hic tonſores atq; chirurgos complures, qui & hic officium exercent ſuum. Maxima balneorum pars ad templa atq; collegia pertinent

s: Once a year the bath servants of Fez go out of the city with trumpets and pipes, gather a wild onion, and carry it to the steam-room door where they hang it in a basket as a lucky omen; Leo takes it for a relic of pre-Islamic sacrifice.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 291, scan p. 294
src.q: balnearum servuli singulis annis festum habent diem … cæpam, ad vaporarii usq; ostium afferunt, ubi cæpam canistello inclusam suspendunt, dicentes hanc fore vaporarii omen felicissimum.

src.l: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), 1632, Africae descriptio IX lib. absoluta (Leiden, Elzevir, 1632)
src.loc: Descriptio Africae III, Fez, printed p. 291, scan p. 294
src.q: they bring the onion up to the entrance of the steam room, where they hang the onion, enclosed in a small basket, saying that this will be a most happy omen for the steam room.
src.qo: balnearum servuli singulis annis festum habent diem … cæpam, ad vaporarii usq; ostium afferunt, ubi cæpam canistello inclusam suspendunt, dicentes hanc fore vaporarii omen felicissimum.

s: Herodotus says Egyptian priests shave the whole body every third day, wear only linen, and wash in cold water twice every day and twice every night.

src.l: Herodotus, 950, Historiae (Greek manuscript, c. 950)
src.loc: Histories II.37, scan p. 139
src.q: λοῦνται δὲ δὶς τῆς ἡμέρης ἑκάστης ψυχρῷ, καὶ δὶς ἑκάστης νυκτός

src.l: Herodotus, 950, Historiae (Greek manuscript, c. 950)
src.loc: Histories II.37, scan p. 139
src.q: They bathe in cold water twice every day and twice every night.
src.qo: λοῦνται δὲ δὶς τῆς ἡμέρης ἑκάστης ψυχρῷ, καὶ δὶς ἑκάστης νυκτός

s: Oertel, after Ludolf, says that on Epiphany (11 Ter; Ethiopic 'Baptism of Christ', Coptic 'the day of the holy immersion') the Ethiopian king with his court, the metropolitan with the clergy, nobles and commoners go down naked into rivers or ponds before sunrise and spend the joyful day immersing themselves.

src.l: Johann Gottfried Oertel, 1746, Theologia Aethiopum (Wittenberg, 1746)
src.loc: Theologia Aethiopum, Locus XIV De Baptismo, printed p. 121, scan p. 149 (sentence begins on scan p. 148)
src.q: Rex cum aulae ſuae primoribus , Me- tropolita cum Clericis , nobiles cum plebeiis, ſenes et iuuenes , in flumina , uel ſtagna nudi (pauciſſimis inter praecipuos exceptis ) ante ortum ſolis deſcendant , ibidemque, merſitando ſeſe, laetum diem agant

src.l: Johann Gottfried Oertel, 1746, Theologia Aethiopum (Wittenberg, 1746)
src.loc: Theologia Aethiopum, Locus XIV De Baptismo, printed p. 121, scan p. 149 (sentence begins on scan p. 148)
src.q: the King with the leaders of his court, the Metropolitan with the Clergy, nobles with commoners, old and young, descend naked (with very few exceptions among the most prominent) into rivers or ponds before sunrise. There, by immersing themselves, they spend a joyful day
src.qo: Rex cum aulae ſuae primoribus , Me- tropolita cum Clericis , nobiles cum plebeiis, ſenes et iuuenes , in flumina , uel ſtagna nudi (pauciſſimis inter praecipuos exceptis ) ante ortum ſolis deſcendant , ibidemque, merſitando ſeſe, laetum diem agant

s: Oertel records the Ethiopic name of baptism, ጥምቀት (timqat), from the root meaning to immerse, and calls it the sacrament of initiation given to infants and adults alike.

src.l: Johann Gottfried Oertel, 1746, Theologia Aethiopum (Wittenberg, 1746)
src.loc: Theologia Aethiopum, Locus XIV De Baptismo, scan p. 138
src.q: primum est *Sa- cramentum Baptismi*, ipsis ጥምቀት: *Tymy- katy* dictum

src.l: Johann Gottfried Oertel, 1746, Theologia Aethiopum (Wittenberg, 1746)
src.loc: Theologia Aethiopum, Locus XIV De Baptismo, scan p. 138
src.q: the first of which, by reason of its order, is the Sacrament of Baptism. It is called Tymykaty by them
src.qo: primum est *Sa- cramentum Baptismi*, ipsis ጥምቀት: *Tymy- katy* dictum

s: Nachtigal says the Tibesti spring's local name Jerike corresponds to Arabic hammam (warm bath, warm spring); its water was said to be too hot to approach for steam, had to cool before people could use it, and was used against diseases of skin, muscles and bones.

src.l: Gustav Nachtigal, 1879, Sahara und Sudan, vol. 1 (Berlin, 1879)
src.loc: Sahara und Sudan I, Tibesti thermal springs, scan p. 415
src.q: Die Thermennatur der berühmten Quelle, welche schon durch den generellen Namen Jerike, der dem arabischen Hammam (warmes Bad, warme Quelle) entspricht, angedeutet wird, kann nicht zweifelhaft sein.

src.l: Gustav Nachtigal, 1879, Sahara und Sudan, vol. 1 (Berlin, 1879)
src.loc: Sahara und Sudan I, Tibesti thermal springs, scan p. 415
src.q: The thermal nature of the famous spring, which is already indicated by the general name Jerike, corresponding to the Arabic Hammam (warm bath, warm spring), cannot be in doubt.
src.qo: Die Thermennatur der berühmten Quelle, welche schon durch den generellen Namen Jerike, der dem arabischen Hammam (warmes Bad, warme Quelle) entspricht, angedeutet wird, kann nicht zweifelhaft sein.

s: Lane says that on the eve of the Gheetās (Epiphany) Coptic men and boys plunged into water to commemorate Christ's baptism, in a church tank blessed by a priest or, more commonly, in the Nile after pouring in holy water from the church.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1895, An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1895 ed.)
src.loc: Modern Egyptians, ch. 'The Copts', printed p. 545, scan p. 575
src.q: To commemorate the baptism of Christ, men—old as well as young—and boys plunge into water … Some churches have a large tank, which is used on this occasion, the water having first been blessed by a priest; but it is a more common practice of the Copts to perform this ceremony (which most of them regard more as an amusement than a religious rite) in the river, pouring in some holy water from the church before they plunge.

s: Pluquet reports that the Copts have large basins in their churches which are filled on Epiphany; the priest blesses the water and plunges children in, the people throw themselves in, and in the countryside the blessing is made on the Nile itself, where the people then bathe.

src.l: François-André-Adrien Pluquet, 1776, Dictionnaire des hérésies, des erreurs et des schismes (1776), vol. 1
src.loc: Dictionnaire des hérésies, art. Cophtes, scan p. 661
src.q: Ils ont dans leurs Egliſes de grands baſſins , ou des lavoirs , qu'ils rempliſſent d'eau le jour de l'Epiphanie , le Prêtre la bénit , y plonge des enfans , & le peuple ſ'y jette

src.l: François-André-Adrien Pluquet, 1776, Dictionnaire des hérésies, des erreurs et des schismes (1776), vol. 1
src.loc: Dictionnaire des hérésies, art. Cophtes, scan p. 661
src.q: They have in their Churches large basins, or washing-places, which they fill with water on the day of Epiphany; the Priest blesses it, plunges children into it, and the people throw themselves into it
src.qo: Ils ont dans leurs Egliſes de grands baſſins , ou des lavoirs , qu'ils rempliſſent d'eau le jour de l'Epiphanie , le Prêtre la bénit , y plonge des enfans , & le peuple ſ'y jette

s: Hernández says the leaves of the plant Tula, applied to the skin, cure leprosy and lichen, especially if the sick person is then taken into the bath the Indians call Temazcalli.

src.l: Francisco Hernández, Nardo Antonio Recchi (ed.), 1651, Rerum medicarum Novae Hispaniae thesaurus
src.loc: Book 3 (plants), the herb Tula, printed p. 129, scan p. 157
src.q: praecipue si aegrotus ducatur in balneum post huiusmodi adhibitam curationem, quam Indi vocant Temazcalli.

src.l: Francisco Hernández, Nardo Antonio Recchi (ed.), 1651, Rerum medicarum Novae Hispaniae thesaurus
src.loc: Book 3 (plants), the herb Tula, printed p. 129, scan p. 157
src.q: Especially if the sick person is taken into a bath after such an application of the cure, which the Indians call Temazcalli.
src.qo: praecipue si aegrotus ducatur in balneum post huiusmodi adhibitam curationem, quam Indi vocant Temazcalli.

s: Molina's Nahuatl dictionary defines temazcalli as a small house like a stove where people bathe.

src.l: Alonso de Molina, 1571, Vocabulario en lengua castellana y mexicana
src.loc: Nahuatl-Spanish part, 'T ante E', scan p. 454
src.q: Temazcalli casilla como estufa, adonde se bañan

s: Molina records a Nahuatl word for the vent of the sweat house: temazcalixtli, 'respiradero de temazcalli'.

src.l: Alonso de Molina, 1571, Vocabulario en lengua castellana y mexicana
src.loc: Nahuatl-Spanish part, 'T ante E', scan p. 454
src.q: Temazcalixtli. respiradero de temazcalli.

s: Molina glosses tetenqui as 'the one who bathes another in the temazcalli', a word for the bath attendant.

src.l: Alonso de Molina, 1571, Vocabulario en lengua castellana y mexicana
src.loc: Nahuatl-Spanish part, scan p. 473
src.q: Tetenqui.el que baña a otro en temazcalli.

s: In the Spanish-Nahuatl half Molina separates ordinary bathing from bathing 'in the hot bath they call temazcalli', which has its own verb, tema.

src.l: Alonso de Molina, 1571, Vocabulario en lengua castellana y mexicana
src.loc: Spanish-Nahuatl part, 'Bañar', scan p. 47
src.q: Bañar en baño caliente, que llaman temazcalli. ni no, tema.

src.qo: Sudadero en el baño lugar / chigoh pibal

s: Landa says the Yucatec Maya bathed their children as soon as they were born, before the head-shaping and the visit to the priest who read the child's fate and gave its name.

src.l: Diego de Landa, Charles Étienne Brasseur de Bourbourg (ed.), 1864, Relation des choses de Yucatan de Diego de Landa (Spanish text with French translation)
src.loc: § on childbirth, scan p. 317
src.q: Nacidos los niños, los bañan luego

src.l: Diego de Landa, Charles Étienne Brasseur de Bourbourg (ed.), 1864, Relation des choses de Yucatan de Diego de Landa (Spanish text with French translation)
src.loc: § on childbirth, scan p. 317
src.q: Once the children were born, they bathed them immediately
src.qo: Nacidos los niños, los bañan luego

s: Cieza describes at the Angoyaco crossing buildings of the Incas and a stone enclosure with a bath of water that flowed there naturally warm, 'of which all the Inca lords were proud'.

src.l: Pedro de Cieza de León, 1922, La crónica del Perú (Madrid, 1922)
src.loc: ch. 85, the road from Jauja to Huamanga, scan p. 318
src.q: estaban edificios de los ingas, y un cercado de piedra, a donde había un baño del agua que salía por aquella parte, que de suyo por naturaleza manaba cálida y conveniente para el baño; de lo cual se preciaron todos los señores ingas

s: Cieza says that wherever the Inca passed he left works behind, and that 'in some places they built baths'.

src.l: Pedro de Cieza de León, 1880, Segunda parte de la crónica del Perú, que trata del señorío de los Incas
src.loc: Señorío, Tupac Inca's progress, scan p. 268
src.q: En algunos lugares edificaron baños, y en otros cotos, y por los desiertos se hicieron grandes casas.

s: Garcilaso says that at the Inca feast Citua, after a day of strict fasting, everyone who had fasted washed their bodies shortly before dawn and rubbed them with dough mixed with blood, as if to cast out all their illnesses.

src.l: Garcilaso de la Vega, el Inca, 1609, Comentarios reales de los Incas
src.loc: Book 7, ch. 6 (the feast Citua), scan p. 347
src.q: todos los que habían ayunado se lavaban los cuerpos y tomaban un poco de la masa mezclada con sangre y la pasaban por la cabeza y rostro, pecho y espalda, brazos y piernas, como que se limpiaban con ella para echar de sus cuerpos todas sus enfermedades.

src.l: Garcilaso de la Vega, el Inca, 1609, Comentarios reales de los Incas
src.loc: Book 7, ch. 6 (the feast Citua), scan p. 347
src.q: all those who had fasted washed their bodies and took a little of the dough mixed with blood and rubbed it over their heads and faces, chests and backs, arms and legs, as if they were cleaning themselves with it to cast out from their bodies all their illnesses.
src.qo: todos los que habían ayunado se lavaban los cuerpos y tomaban un poco de la masa mezclada con sangre y la pasaban por la cabeza y rostro, pecho y espalda, brazos y piernas, como que se limpiaban con ella para echar de sus cuerpos todas sus enfermedades.

s: Garcilaso says the head of each house then smeared the dough on the threshold of the street door, as a sign that the washing had been done in that house.

s: Léry says the Tupinamba women, at every spring and clear river they came to, crouched on the bank or went in and poured water over their heads with both hands, washing and plunging the whole body, as much as twelve times in a day.

s: The Book of Ceremonies describes the emperors bathing at the holy Lousma of Blachernai: they undress in the dressing rooms, put on gold linen cloths and enter, venerate the silver icons in the pool (kolymbos), light candles before a marble Theotokos that pours holy water from her hands, sign themselves and bathe, then change into gold-woven linens.

s: The Yuan monastic code Chixiu Baizhang qinggui gives the bath master (知浴) his rhythm: when the bath is opened (開浴) he hangs the 'bath open' board before the midday meal; in the cold months there is a bath every five days, in the hot season a daily rinse of sweat (淋汗); he lays out the bath-room with hand towels, face basins, slippers and foot-cloths.

src.l: Dongyang Dehui 東陽德煇 (comp.), 1442, 勅修百丈清規 (Imperially revised Pure Rules of Baizhang)
src.loc: 知浴 (bath master), scan 91

s: In the Baizhang qinggui the bath begins with the holy ones: a little hot water is put in the tubs, incense is burnt and the 'holy' are invited to bathe; then the drum sounds four times, and at the first the monks enter, at the second the heads of offices, at the third the novices (行者), at the fourth the labourers; the abbot bathes behind a screen.

src.l: Dongyang Dehui 東陽德煇 (comp.), 1442, 勅修百丈清規 (Imperially revised Pure Rules of Baizhang)

s: The Baizhang qinggui has a small board hung inside the bath-room, with a tablet beside it reading: one stroke on the board, add hot water; two, add cold; three, stop. The bather signals the stokers outside by sound.

s: The Baizhang qinggui's daily rules tell the monk how to undress for the bath: enter by the lower door with the bath kit in the right hand, bow, hang the five-strip robe's towel on the pole, open the bath bundle, take off the lower skirt first and wrap the foot-cloth round the body before tying on the bath skirt; 'clean and defiled must be kept apart, upper and lower garments' (觸淨須分上下衣).

s: The Baizhang qinggui forbids, in the bath: going in barefoot; taking the upper places where the senior monks sit (wait in the lower part of the room); splashing others; soaking the feet in the tub; urinating in the room; laughing and talking; standing up to pour from the tub over oneself; letting the foot-cloth leave the body. Those with sores, moxa burns or scabies ointment bathe last.

src.loc: 日用軌範, bathing, scan 157
src.q: 不得赤腳入浴須於下間空處待次而浴不得占頭 首老宿坐處 … 不得以湯水濺人身上不得桶内 泡腳不得室内小遺不得架腳桶上不得笑語 … 腳布不得離身 … 或有瘡或洗灸瘡或使疥藥宜後入浴

s: After the bath, says the Baizhang qinggui, the monk bows left and right, sits a little on the platform facing the wall, dresses his upper body under the robe before taking off the wet bath skirt, folds it inside the foot-cloth so the bundle stays dry, and in cold months warms himself at the brazier without drying shoes or clothes over it.

src.l: Dongyang Dehui 東陽德煇 (comp.), 1442, 勅修百丈清規 (Imperially revised Pure Rules of Baizhang)
src.loc: 日用軌範, bathing, scan 157
src.q: 出浴揖左右上床面壁少 坐先着上衣并直裰都遮了下地却着下裳解浴裙 以腳布摺浴裙内恐濕浴袱 … 寒月向火先 坐爐圈上 … 不得炙鞋焙屩烘衣裳

s: For the Buddha's birthday the Baizhang qinggui has the stores office set up a flower pavilion with the image of the newborn Buddha in a basin of fragrant water (香湯) and two small ladles; the abbot leads the assembly to bathe the Buddha with the verse 'I now bathe all the Tathāgatas … may beings of the five defilements be freed from dirt'.

src.l: Dongyang Dehui 東陽德煇 (comp.), 1442, 勅修百丈清規 (Imperially revised Pure Rules of Baizhang)
src.loc: 佛降誕, scan 32
src.q: 庫司嚴設花亭中置佛降生像於香湯盆內安 二小杓 … 我今灌沐諸如來淨智莊嚴功德聚 五濁衆生令離垢同證如來淨法身

s: The Gezhi jingyuan quotes Lang Ying's Qixiu leigao (16th c.) on the public bath-house of Wu (Suzhou): a pool lined with big stones under a vault of brick; behind it a great cauldron connected to the pool; a winch draws water through a hole in the wall to fill it; one man does nothing but stoke; the water mixes into a boiling bath called the 'mixed hall' (混堂), with 'Fragrant Water' (香水) on the sign over the door, and any man who pays the keeper one coin may go in and wash.

src.l: 陳元龍 Chen Yuanlong, 1896, 格致鏡原 (Gezhi jingyuan)
src.loc: 卷十九 宮室類 浴室, quoting Lang Ying's 七修類藁, scan 431
src.q: 吳俗甃大石為池穹幕以磚後為巨釜 令與池通轆轤引水穴壁而貯馬一人專執爨池水相吞遂成沸湯名曰混堂 榜其門則曰香水男子納一錢於主人皆得入澡焉

s: The Gezhi jingyuan quotes the Shiyi ji on the bath of Shi Hu (4th c.): banks of brass and jade-like stone, ladles of amber, gauze bags of mixed fragrances steeped in the water; in hard frost dozens of bronze coiled dragons, each of several tens of catties, were heated red and thrown in so the pool stayed warm, the 'Pool of Scorched Dragons'.

src.l: 陳元龍 Chen Yuanlong, 1896, 格致鏡原 (Gezhi jingyuan)
src.loc: 卷十九 浴室, quoting 拾遺記, scan 431
src.q: 石虎 為浴室用鍮石碔砆為堤岸以琥珀為餅杓又以紗縠為囊盛百雜香漬于水 中嚴氷之時作銅屈龍數十枚各重數十斤燒如火色投水中則池水恒温名 曰焦龍池

s: The Gezhi jingyuan quotes Tang Geng's (Tang Zixi) record of the springs at the Footprint-of-Buddha cloister near Huizhou: two springs a few steps apart, the eastern hot past touching with a finger, the western cold as snow; the hot is let down with the cold until it is mild enough to bathe.

src.l: 陳元龍 Chen Yuanlong, 1896, 格致鏡原 (Gezhi jingyuan)
src.loc: 溫泉, quoting 唐子西遊湯泉記, scan 166
src.q: 院中 涌二泉其東所謂湯泉其西雪如也二泉相去步武間而東泉熱甚殆不可觸 指以西泉解之然後調適可浴

s: Zhao Xuemin's Supplement to the Compendium of Materia Medica (1765) explains the 'mixed hall' (混堂) as today's bath-pool with heated water; when many bathe, filth and grime collect and the vapour of people steeps the room, so that weak people who meet it faint, and the place is called the 'fainting hall' (暈堂).

src.l: Zhao Xuemin 趙學敏, 1765, 本草綱目拾遺 (Supplement to the Compendium of Materia Medica), 卷一 水部
src.loc: 卷一 水部 混堂水, scan 95
src.q: 混堂今浴池燒水浴者人多則穢濁積垢使然人 氣薰漬體虛者觸之昏暈名曰暈堂

s: Lu Rong (15th c.) describes the Lintong hot spring at the foot of Mount Li, the old Huaqing palace: only the pool remains, roofed with a few bays and lined with brick and stone, its water evenly warm and clear enough to see a hair; officials control it, so only the noble can bathe there; outside it the spring is led off into two 'mixed halls' (混堂), for men and for women, shared by the people.

src.l: Lu Rong 陸容, 1494, 菽園雜記 卷一 (Miscellaneous Records from the Bean Garden, juan 1)
src.loc: 卷一, scans 18-19
src.q: 溫泉在臨潼縣驪山北麓即唐之華清宮故址

src.l: Lu Rong 陸容, 1494, 菽園雜記 卷一 (Miscellaneous Records from the Bean Garden, juan 1)
src.loc: 卷一, scans 18-19
src.q: 上覆屋數楹四周甃以甓石其水寒煖適 調清徹可鑑絲髮 … 然以官府掌之非貴宦無由得 浴其外别引泉為男女混堂二處則居民共之

s: The Puji fang (1406) treats scabies in the bath-house: the patient goes into the bath-house until sweat comes, then into the hot water, scratches the sores open and rubs in the medicine with clean oil, and does this washing and rubbing three times inside the bath-house before coming out.

src.l: Zhu Su 朱橚 (ed.), 1406, 普濟方 卷二百八十 (Prescriptions for Universal Relief, juan 280)
src.loc: 卷二百八十 疥瘡, scan 24
src.q: 入浴堂内令汗出便休下湯浴将疥抓破用前藥以 清油搽之入浴堂内洗就浴堂内如此擦洗三次方 才出浴

s: A Song anecdote (in Pan Yongyin's Song bai leichao) describes the official Pu Chuanzheng's washing regime: small and great face-washes, small and great foot-washes, small and great baths; a small bath used three hu of water and five or six attendants, a great bath five hu and eight or nine; daily two face-washes and two foot-washes, a small bath every other day and a great bath on the alternate day.

src.l: Pan Yongyin 潘永因, 1669, 宋稗類鈔 (Categorized Anecdotes of the Song Dynasty), juan 15 part
src.loc: scan 182
src.q: 大洗面小洗面大濯足小濯足大 澡浴小澡浴 … 小澡浴 湯用三斛人用五六大澡浴湯用五斛人用八九每 曰兩洗面兩濯足間曰一小浴又間曰一大浴

s: Gao Lian (1591) describes the Buddha's birthday (4th month, 8th day) in Hangzhou: monks and nuns put a bronze image in a small basin of sugar-and-fruit water under a flower canopy and carry it with cymbals and drums to the houses of the rich, who pour water over the image with small ladles and give alms.

src.l: Gao Lian 高濂, 1591, 遵生八牋 (Eight Treatises on Following the Principles of Life)
src.loc: 四時 (summer customs), 寺院浴佛, scan 116
src.q: 四月八日為佛誕辰諸寺院各有浴佛㑹僧尼競以小 盆貯銅像浸以糖菓之水覆以花棚鐃鼓交迎徧往邸 第富室以小杓澆灌佛身以求施利

s: The Tianzhong ji quotes the Jingchu suishi ji: on the 8th of the 4th month the monasteries of Jingchu hold vegetarian feasts and bathe the Buddha with five-coloured fragrant water (五色香水), and with the Gaoseng zhuan it begins the list of colours: dūliang fragrance for the blue water.

src.l: Chen Yaowen 陳耀文, 1569, 天中記 卷五 (Records of Tianzhong, juan 5)
src.loc: 卷五 四月八日, scan 32
src.q: 浴佛荊楚人以四月八日諸寺設齋以五色香水浴佛 共作龍華㑹 歲時 記 四月八日浴佛以都梁香為青色水

s: The Peiwen yunfu quotes the Dongjing menghua lu: on the Buddha's birthday the ten great Chan monasteries of the Northern Song capital each hold a Buddha-bathing feast and boil fragrant medicinal sugar water, which they give to one another, called 'Buddha-bath water' (浴佛水).

src.l: Zhang Yushu 張玉書 et al., 1711, 佩文韻府 (Peiwen Rhyme Treasury), the 水 rhyme volume
src.loc: 浴佛水, scan 133
src.q: 浴佛水 東京夢華錄 四月八日佛 生日十大禪院各有浴佛齋㑹煎香藥糖水相遺 名曰丨丨丨

s: The Tianzhong ji quotes the biography of Li Shi: under the Tang emperor, on winter excursions to Xinfeng the court climbed Mount Li, and the courtiers were granted a bath in the hot-spring pool and given fragrant powder and orchid oil (香粉蘭澤), while the emperor wrote poems and the scholars matched them.

src.l: Chen Yaowen 陳耀文, 1569, 天中記 卷五 (Records of Tianzhong, juan 5)
src.loc: 卷五, 浴湯池 (from the 李適傳), scan 145
src.q: 浴湯池唐高宗時凡天子享㑹冬幸新豐歴白鹿觀上 驪山賜浴湯池給香粉蘭澤帝賦詩學士皆屬和

s: Li Shizhen's Bencao gangmu, under 'warm water' (溫湯, hot springs), quotes Chen Cangqi that the springs treat wind diseases, cramps, numb skin and scabies, but leave the bather greatly weakened, so that one should not go in without illness; and Wang Ying that at Lushan the adepts sent people with scabies, leprosy and syphilitic sores to eat their fill, enter the pool and soak long until they sweat, and they recovered within ten days.

src.l: Li Shizhen 李時珍, 1655, 本草綱目 (Compendium of Materia Medica), 水部 溫湯
src.loc: 卷五 水部 溫湯, scan 925
src.q: 入浴 浴訖當大虛儻可隨病與藥及飲食補養非有病 人不宜輕入 … 頴曰廬山有溫泉方士往往教患疥癬風癲 楊梅瘡者飽食入池乆浴得汗出乃止旬日 自愈

s: The Jesuit-Chinese Taixi shuifa (1612) explains why hot springs cure: the water takes the essence of the sulphur it rises through, and of those who use springs to cure, nine in ten fume and bathe and one in ten drink, because bathing keeps the heat-poison out of the stomach while its force still reaches the pores.

src.l: Sabatino de Ursis 熊三拔, Xu Guangqi 徐光啟, 1612, 泰西水法 (Western Hydraulics), vols. 4-6
src.loc: 溫泉 第一, scan 11
src.q: 溫泉 出於硫黃 … 又溫泉療病用之薰浴者什九用之湯飲者 什一薰沐者其熱毒不致入於腸胃而性力却能達於 腠理則利多而害少焉

s: Zhang Bangji (12th c.) sorts hot springs into two kinds: most are very hot with a fierce smell and are 'sulphur springs'; but one near Pingke town is only mildly warm, can be touched, and has no fiery breath, and is called a 'cinnabar spring'; people say two beauties once bathed there and the strange fragrance lasted days.

src.l: Zhang Bangji 張邦基, 1131, 墨莊漫錄 (Miscellaneous Records of the Ink Studio)
src.loc: scan 111
src.q: 湯泉有處甚多大熱而氣烈乃硫黃湯也唯利州褒禪 山相近地名平痾鎮湯泉溫溫可探而不作火氣 云是朱砂湯也人傳昔有兩美人來浴既去異香郁 郁累日不散

s: The Mingyi lei'an records a diagnosis made in the bath-room: a physician sat the patient by the fire there and washed him with fried scallion water; heat illness would sweat in the warm room without the sore throat easing, cold would give no sweat; no sweat came, so he gave ephedra in the bath-room and a great sweat followed, and the case is offered as a general test.

src.l: Jiang Guan 江瓘, 1552, 名醫類案 卷七 (Classified Cases of Famous Physicians, juan 7)
src.loc: 卷七, scan 100
src.q: 驗得寒熱 浴室中坐火用炒木蔥湯沐浴若是病熱則此煖處 必有汗 … 遂入沐淋洗而無汗就浴室中服麻黃一服 須臾大汗 … 凡辨熱病與 感寒皆可用此法

s: On Mencius' saying that an ugly man who fasts and bathes (齋戒沐浴) may sacrifice to Shangdi, the commentary explains that even the beautiful Xi Shi with a dirty cloth on her head would make people cover their noses, while the ugliest man, if he fasts, bathes and cleans his body, can serve God.

src.l: Zhao Qi 趙岐 (comm.), Sun Shi 孫奭 (subcomm.), 1000, 孟子注疏 卷八 (Commentary and Subcommentary on Mencius, juan 8)
src.loc: Mencius 4B.25, 注疏, scan 56
src.q: 如惡人雖曰至醜然能齋戒沐浴自潔淨其身則亦 可以供事上帝矣

s: Su Shi's commentary on the Book of Documents explains King Cheng's washing before his last command: to issue a great command one should fast and bathe (齋戒沐浴), but the king was ill and could not, so he only washed his hands (洮) and his face (頮).

src.l: Su Shi 蘇軾, 1100, 書傳 卷十四至十七 (Commentary on the Book of Documents)
src.loc: 顧命 (Gu ming), scan 109
src.q: 發大命當齋戒沐浴今有疾不能洮頮水而已洮盥 也頮頮面也

s: Shen Kuo tells of Wang Anshi's dark face: a physician said it was dirt, not illness, and offered bath-bean powder (澡豆) to wash it; Wang answered that Heaven had made him dark, and what could bath-beans do about that.

src.l: Shen Kuo 沈括, 1088, 夢溪筆談 (Dream Pool Essays)
src.loc: scan 85
src.q: 曰此垢汙非疾也進澡豆令公頮面公曰天生黑於 予澡豆其如予何

s: The illustrated Ming life of the Buddha, quoting the Sutra on Bathing the Buddha (灌佛經), says that at the prince's birth the Brahmā heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and the Four Heavenly Kings each bathed him with twelve kinds of fragrant water (十二種香湯); the eighth of the fourth month is used because between spring and summer 'poisonous vapours have not yet spread, it is neither cold nor hot', and to bathe the image after the Buddha's death brings merit beyond counting.

src.l: Baocheng 寶成 (comp.), 1480, 釋氏源流應化事蹟 (Shishi yuanliu yinghua shiji, Illustrated Life of the Buddha)
src.loc: 浴佛形像, scan 172
src.q: 各持十二種香湯浴太子身 … 佛言。所以用四月八日者。以春夏之際。殃罪悉畢。萬物普生。毒氣未行。不寒不熱。時氣和適。正是佛生之日 … 浴佛形像。如佛在時。得福無量

s: Salzmann's rules for a spa cure: on arriving do not bathe hastily and hard but add an hour from day to day; in hot weather bathe in the morning and late evening; and bathe at sunrise or a little before.

src.l: Gregor Salzmann, 1538, Ain new gar schoen und nutzlichs buechlin von allen wildbeder natur wirckung unnd aygenschafft
src.loc: 'Die Regel wie man Baden soll', rules 2 and 4, scans 13-14 (this quote: scan 13)
src.q: Die ander Regel / So jr inn das Bad kumpt / solt jr nit eylends unnd streng Baden / sonder von tag zu tag ain stund zu geben.

src.l: Gregor Salzmann, 1538, Ain new gar schoen und nutzlichs buechlin von allen wildbeder natur wirckung unnd aygenschafft
src.loc: 'Die Regel wie man Baden soll', rules 2 and 4, scans 13-14 (this quote: scan 14)
src.q: Die vierdt Regel/ Die stund so ains Baden will/ sol sein die stund so die Sonn auffgeht/ oder ain wenig daruor

src.l: Gregor Salzmann, 1538, Ain new gar schoen und nutzlichs buechlin von allen wildbeder natur wirckung unnd aygenschafft
src.loc: 'Die Regel wie man Baden soll', rules 2 and 4, scans 13-14 (this quote: scan 13)
src.q: The second rule: when you come into the bath, you should not bathe hurriedly and strictly, but from day to day add an hour.
src.qo: Die ander Regel / So jr inn das Bad kumpt / solt jr nit eylends unnd streng Baden / sonder von tag zu tag ain stund zu geben.

s: Before going into the bath one should empty the bowels and bladder, or the bath draws the superfluities into the weak limbs; and while sitting in the water one should neither eat nor drink.

src.l: Gregor Salzmann, 1538, Ain new gar schoen und nutzlichs buechlin von allen wildbeder natur wirckung unnd aygenschafft
src.loc: Rules 5 and 6, scan 14
src.q: Die fünfft Regel/ Wann ains in das bad gehn will/ so sol es sich vorhin rainigen von überflüssigkeiten der Stülgäng/ des Harms/ der spaichel et cetera. … Die sechst Regel/ ist/ dieweil ir in dem wasser sizt/ so solt ir weder essen noch trincken

src.l: Gregor Salzmann, 1538, Ain new gar schoen und nutzlichs buechlin von allen wildbeder natur wirckung unnd aygenschafft
src.loc: Rules 5 and 6, scan 14
src.q: The sixth rule is: while you sit in the water, you should neither eat nor drink.
src.qo: Die fünfft Regel/ Wann ains in das bad gehn will/ so sol es sich vorhin rainigen von überflüssigkeiten der Stülgäng/ des Harms/ der spaichel et cetera. … Die sechst Regel/ ist/ dieweil ir in dem wasser sizt/ so solt ir weder essen noch trincken

s: Coming out of the bath one should cover oneself well with white cloths so the air does not reach the opened body, then lie in a bed well covered and sleep and sweat, which settles the body and brings the loosened superfluities out in sweat.

src.l: Gregor Salzmann, 1538, Ain new gar schoen und nutzlichs buechlin von allen wildbeder natur wirckung unnd aygenschafft
src.loc: Rules 8 and 9, scan 15
src.q: Die acht Regel / wann ains auß dem Bad geht / so soll es sich wol bedecken mitt weyssen thüchern / das der lufft nit an ains geh … Die neündt Regel / so ains auß dem Bad gangen ist / das leg sich in ain bedt / wol zugedeckt / und schlaff und schwiz

src.l: Gregor Salzmann, 1538, Ain new gar schoen und nutzlichs buechlin von allen wildbeder natur wirckung unnd aygenschafft
src.loc: Rules 8 and 9, scan 15
src.q: The ninth rule: when one has gone out of the bath, one should lie in a bed, well covered, and sleep and sweat
src.qo: Die acht Regel / wann ains auß dem Bad geht / so soll es sich wol bedecken mitt weyssen thüchern / das der lufft nit an ains geh … Die neündt Regel / so ains auß dem Bad gangen ist / das leg sich in ain bedt / wol zugedeckt / und schlaff und schwiz

s: Before eating after the bath one should walk back and forth for a while to drive out the vapours raised by the bath's heat; someone too weak to walk should have the limbs softly rubbed with a warm cloth.

src.l: Gregor Salzmann, 1538, Ain new gar schoen und nutzlichs buechlin von allen wildbeder natur wirckung unnd aygenschafft
src.loc: Rule 10, scan 15
src.q: Die X. Regel / Eh und der mensch ysset / soll er sich ain weil etwas üben / mithin und her gehn / auff das die dempf / und windigkaiten so von des Bads hitz erhept seind / außgetriben werden / ob ainer aber so schwach wär / das er nit gehn möcht / so laß er im die glider senfft reiben mit ainem warmen thüch

src.l: Gregor Salzmann, 1538, Ain new gar schoen und nutzlichs buechlin von allen wildbeder natur wirckung unnd aygenschafft
src.loc: Rule 10, scan 15
src.q: before the person eats, he should exercise himself for a while, walk back and forth
src.qo: Die X. Regel / Eh und der mensch ysset / soll er sich ain weil etwas üben / mithin und her gehn / auff das die dempf / und windigkaiten so von des Bads hitz erhept seind / außgetriben werden / ob ainer aber so schwach wär / das er nit gehn möcht / so laß er im die glider senfft reiben mit ainem warmen thüch

s: After a meal one should not go into the bath until three hours have passed, and during a course of bathing one should avoid 'the work of love', because both waste the moisture the bath opens.

src.l: Gregor Salzmann, 1538, Ain new gar schoen und nutzlichs buechlin von allen wildbeder natur wirckung unnd aygenschafft
src.loc: Rules 12 and 13, scans 16-17 (this quote: scan 16)
src.q: Die XII. Regel ist / So ainer das mal genomen hat / so sol er nit inn das Bad gehn / ehe iij. stund vergangen seind

src.l: Gregor Salzmann, 1538, Ain new gar schoen und nutzlichs buechlin von allen wildbeder natur wirckung unnd aygenschafft
src.loc: Rules 12 and 13, scans 16-17 (this quote: scan 17)
src.q: Die XIII. Regel / iſt / das aines ſol meyden das werck der liebe/ dieweil ains badet/

src.l: Gregor Salzmann, 1538, Ain new gar schoen und nutzlichs buechlin von allen wildbeder natur wirckung unnd aygenschafft
src.loc: Rules 12 and 13, scans 16-17 (this quote: scan 17)
src.q: The thirteenth rule is that one should avoid the work of love while one is bathing.
src.qo: Die XIII. Regel / iſt / das aines ſol meyden das werck der liebe/ dieweil ains badet/

s: At Überkingen five hours of bathing a day, two in the morning and three in the afternoon, is enough for those who also drink the spring; those who only bathe may reach seven hours, but must increase the hours gradually; sitting in the water all day is wrong, for the bath also works when one leaves at the right time, lies in bed, rests and sweats.

src.l: Jacob Eckholt, 1651, Kurtze Beschreibung Deß Saurbronnens zu Uberkingen
src.loc: On bathing, scan 30
src.q: Wann man auff die fünff Stund deß Tags kompt / kompt Vormittag auff zwen / vnnd Nachmittag auff drey / wirds genug seyn … dann das Bad würckt nicht nun wann man im Wasser sitzt / sonder auch wann man zu rechter Zeit außgeht / sich ins Beth legt / darin- nen außruhet / / vnd etwan ein Schweiß thut

src.l: Jacob Eckholt, 1651, Kurtze Beschreibung Deß Saurbronnens zu Uberkingen
src.loc: On bathing, scan 30
src.q: For the bath takes effect not only when one sits in the water, but also when one leaves at the proper time, lies down in bed, rests therein, perhaps has a sweat, and waits it out.
src.qo: Wann man auff die fünff Stund deß Tags kompt / kompt Vormittag auff zwen / vnnd Nachmittag auff drey / wirds genug seyn … dann das Bad würckt nicht nun wann man im Wasser sitzt / sonder auch wann man zu rechter Zeit außgeht / sich ins Beth legt / darin- nen außruhet / / vnd etwan ein Schweiß thut

s: Eckholt says one should neither go into nor come out of the bath too hot, and should finish early enough to lie down in bed and rest and recover before eating.

src.l: Jacob Eckholt, 1651, Kurtze Beschreibung Deß Saurbronnens zu Uberkingen
src.loc: Scan 31
src.q: Man soll auch nicht gar zu heiß ein- vnd nicht gar zu heyß außgehn / auch so zeitlich daß man sich ins Beth legen / außruhen / vnd noch vor dem Essen sich ermundteren könne.

src.l: Jacob Eckholt, 1651, Kurtze Beschreibung Deß Saurbronnens zu Uberkingen
src.loc: Scan 31
src.q: One should also not enter entirely too hot, nor leave entirely too hot
src.qo: Man soll auch nicht gar zu heiß ein- vnd nicht gar zu heyß außgehn / auch so zeitlich daß man sich ins Beth legen / außruhen / vnd noch vor dem Essen sich ermundteren könne.

s: At the new mineral bath of Neumarkt, Rhumel sets the bath hours by age and temperament: men bathe shorter and colder, women warmer and longer; one climbs from half an hour to at most six hours a day and steps down again just as gradually at the end; bathe in the morning fasting and in the evening after digestion, and never sleep in the tub; spring and autumn (May, June, September, October) are the best seasons.

src.l: Johann Conrad Rhumel, 1598, Gründliche Beschreibung Des Newerbauten Minerischen Bads Der Churf. Stadt Newenmarckt in der Obern Pfaltz
src.loc: Scan 8
src.q: Die Männer sollen kürzer vnnd kälter/ die Weiber aber wärmer vnd lenger baden/nicht zu vil gehling anfangs/ sondern algemach etlich zeit auff ein halbe/eine/ zwo/drey/vier/ auff daß höchst 6. stund ein tag/immer hinauff steigen: Also auch zu ende nicht geschwind hinab fallen/ sondern algemach auffhören … In der Wannen sol aller schlaff verhütet

s: At Ems a patient should rest one day after the journey, take a gentle purge the next, and begin the bath cure the morning after; if there is much bad blood a vein is opened first; the first bath is about a quarter of an hour in the morning.

src.l: Johann Daniel Horstius, 1676, Embser Bades beschreibung
src.loc: 'Genuinus usus Thermarum', scan 7
src.q: Wann aber ein Patient zu Embs anlanget / soll er einen Tag wegen der Reiß außruhen/ fol- genden Tag eine Purgation brauchen / und nach selbigem Tag deß Morgens mit der Bad-Cur ei- nen Anfang machen.

src.l: Johann Daniel Horstius, 1676, Embser Bades beschreibung
src.loc: 'Genuinus usus Thermarum', scan 7
src.q: When, however, a patient arrives at Ems, he should rest for one day on account of the journey, take a purgation on the following day, and after that day begin the bath cure in the morning.
src.qo: Wann aber ein Patient zu Embs anlanget / soll er einen Tag wegen der Reiß außruhen/ fol- genden Tag eine Purgation brauchen / und nach selbigem Tag deß Morgens mit der Bad-Cur ei- nen Anfang machen.

s: At Teplitz Leder advises lying down after the bath and covering oneself warmly so the warmed blood settles and the sweat and vapours raised by the bath draw out gradually, and going into the bath always on an empty stomach, or after a few spoonfuls of soup.

src.l: Mattheus Leder, 1717, Kurtze Beschreibung Des Heilsamen Warmen Bades Der Hoch-Gräffl. Clarischen Stadt, Töplitz
src.loc: Scan 32
src.q: der legen und sich fein warm zudecken, denn auff diese Arth richtet das erwärmte Geblüthe nicht alleine in seine ordentlich Circulation sich wieder ein, sondern der Schweiß und die Dünste, so von des Bades Wärme entstanden, können auch fein nach und nach vollends heraus ziehen; es ist auch rathsam und dienlich, daß man jederzeit mit einem leeren Magen in das Bad gehe

s: The 1656 bath ordinance of the Laimnau bath-house forbids disputes about religion and other vexing talk contrary to the cure, forbids any guest to drive another from the room, tub and place he has ordered, and asks all guests to keep quiet and still with one another.

src.l: Laurentius Grubenmann, 1656, Beschreibung ... deß nutzlichen und hailsamben Laimenawer Badwassers, die Badhutten genandt ... Sambt einer Badordnung
src.loc: Badordnung, articles VI-VIII, scan 17

s: The house- and bath-master must see that the bath attendants supply warm and cold bath water, keep the bath hut clean, scrub and wash the tubs daily and fill them with fresh water so that bad smell and filth are prevented, and urge the guests themselves to cleanliness.

src.l: Laurentius Grubenmann, 1656, Beschreibung ... deß nutzlichen und hailsamben Laimenawer Badwassers, die Badhutten genandt ... Sambt einer Badordnung

s: The Laimnau bath hut is large and partitioned so that men and women, and above all those with unclean, hereditary diseases, have their own tubs and places; the spring is enclosed and covered against rain, smells of sulphur, and is cold, so it must be heated for bathing.

s: Comenius's school-book describes the bath: wash off dirt in a tub, or go into the steam room (vaporarium), climb onto the sweat-bench (sudatorium) and press out sweat, rub off the scrapings with a haircloth and wipe with linen, and pass from the warm bath to the cold or the reverse.

src.l: Jan Amos Comenius, 1666, Janua linguarum reserata
src.q: balnea sunt eò, ut sqvalores deluamus labro: aut vaporarium ingressi, in sudatorium conscendamus, & sudorem eliciamus, unaqve strigmenta cilicio defricemus

s: At St Wenefrede's Well in Holywell, Pennant saw in summer a few pilgrims (mostly from Lancashire, and most of them women) standing in the water up to their chins for hours in prayer, or going round the polygonal well, or threading the arch between well and well a prescribed number of times.

src.l: Thomas Pennant, 1778, A Tour in Wales, MDCCLXX, vol. 1
src.loc: St Wenefrede's Well, printed p. 36, scan 56
src.q: In the summer, still a few are to be seen in the water in deep devotion up to their chins for hours, sending up their prayers, or performing a number of evolutions round the polygonal well; or threading the arch between well and well a prescribed number of times.

s: Over the Holywell spring hang votive crutches, barrows and other proofs of cures, given by Protestants as well as Catholics; Pennant himself puts the cures down to the waters having 'every good quality attendant on cold baths'.

src.l: Thomas Pennant, 1778, A Tour in Wales, MDCCLXX, vol. 1
src.loc: Scans 55 and 57 (this quote: scan 55)
src.q: the votive crutches, the barrows, and other proofs of cures, to this moment remain as evidences pendent over the well. The saint is equally propitious to Protestants and Catholics

src.l: Thomas Pennant, 1778, A Tour in Wales, MDCCLXX, vol. 1
src.loc: Scans 55 and 57 (this quote: scan 57)
src.q: The waters are indisputably endowed with every good quality attendant on cold baths

s: At Loch Siant Well on Skye people bound by a vow drink the water, then go three times round the well sunwise, east to west (the Dessil), and on leaving never fail to put a small offering on the stone that covers the well.

src.l: Martin Martin, 1703, A Description of the Western Islands of Scotland
src.loc: Skye, Loch Siant Well, printed p. 140, scan 177
src.q: Several of the common People oblige themselves by a Vow to come to this Well, and make the ordinary Touer about it, call'd Dessil, which is performed thus; they move thrice round the Well proceeding Sun-ways from East to West and so on, this is done after drinking of the Water, and when one goes away from the Well, it's a never failing custom, to leave some small offering on the Stone which covers the Well

s: In the Western Isles children are bathed all over every morning and evening, some in cold and some in warm water, the warm more commonly.

src.l: Martin Martin, 1703, A Description of the Western Islands of Scotland
src.loc: Scan 233
src.q: they are bath'd all over every Morning and Evening, some in cold, some in warm water; but the latter is most commonly us'd

s: Islanders tired from travel bathe their feet in warm water in which red moss has been boiled and rub them with it going to bed; Martin adds that the old custom of rubbing the body with a hand warmed at the fire is now laid aside.

src.l: Martin Martin, 1703, A Description of the Western Islands of Scotland
src.loc: Scan 234
src.q: they fail not to bath their Feet in warm water, wherein red Moss has been boil'd, and rub them with it going to bed.  THE ancient Custom of rubbing the Body by a warm hand opposite to the fire, is now laid aside

s: Celsus gives the bath sequence for anyone tired who is about to eat: first sit in the tepidarium, then after resting a little go in and down into the hot tub (solium), then be anointed with much oil and gently rubbed, then go down into the tub again; afterwards foment the mouth with hot water, then cold. A very hot bath is not suitable for them.

src.l: Aulus Cornelius Celsus, 1478, De medicina (editio princeps, Florence 1478)
src.loc: Book 1, ch. 3 (after fatigue), scan p. 38
src.q: si est: ante omnia intepidario residere: deinde ubi paulum conquie uerunt: intrare & descendere in folium: tum multo oleo ungi/ leniter que perfricari: iterum in folium descendere. Post hæc os aqua calida fouere: deinde frigida. Balneum his feruens idoneum non est.

s: For a weak head Celsus says: in the bath first sweat a little in the tepidarium still under one's clothes, be anointed there, then pass into the caldarium; after sweating do not go down into the tub but pour plenty of hot water over the head and the whole body, then tepid, then cold, longer on the head than elsewhere.

src.l: Aulus Cornelius Celsus, 1478, De medicina (editio princeps, Florence 1478)
src.loc: Book 1, ch. 4 (a weak head), scan p. 44
src.q: sub ueste primum paulum intepidario infudare: ibi ungi: tum tranfire incalidarium. ubi fudabit: in folium non descendere: sed multa calida aqua pcaput fe totum pfundere: tum repida de infrigida. diutiusque ea caput quam ceteras partes pfundere

s: Celsus says sweat is drawn in two ways, by dry heat or by the bath; dry heat means hot sand, the laconicum, the oven (clibanus), and natural sweating places where hot vapour from the earth is shut in a building, as above Baiae in the myrtle groves.

src.l: Aulus Cornelius Celsus, 1478, De medicina (editio princeps, Florence 1478)
src.loc: Book 2, 'De sudore', scan p. 83
src.q: Sudor etiam duobus modis elicitur: aut sicco calore: aut balneo. Siccus calor est harenae calidae et laconici et clibani et quarundam naturalium sudationes: ubi e terra psufus calidus uapor aedificio includitur: sicut super baias in myrtetis habemus.

src.l: Aulus Cornelius Celsus, 1478, De medicina (editio princeps, Florence 1478)
src.loc: Book 2, 'De sudore', scan p. 83
src.q: Sweat is also elicited in two ways: either by dry heat or by a bath.

s: Celsus says the bath has a double use, sometimes after fevers to begin fuller food and stronger wine, sometimes to remove the fever itself, and it is applied where the surface of the skin should be relaxed and corrupt humour drawn out.

src.l: Aulus Cornelius Celsus, 1478, De medicina (editio princeps, Florence 1478)
src.loc: Book 2, 'De sudore', scan p. 83

s: Describing the Greek palaestra after Vitruvius, Palladio lists the rooms in order: the place for oiling, the cold room for undressing, the tepid room with its fire, the hot room with the laconicum ('the place where they sweated') on one side and the hot wash on the other; the ancients wanted, 'imitating nature', that one should not go straight from the cold room into the hot but by way of the tepid.

src.l: Andrea Palladio, 1570, I quattro libri dell'architettura
src.loc: Book 3, the Greek palaestra, scan p. 196
src.q: haueua questa stanza da vna parte il laconico (era questo il luogo, oue sudauano) e dall' altra la stanza per la calda lauatione. Percioche vollero quei prudenti huomini, imitando la na- tura, laqual da vn estremo freddo ad vn' estremo caldo có i suoi mezzi ci conduce, che nó subito dal la stāza fredda si entrasse nella calda, ma col mezo della tepida.

src.l: Andrea Palladio, 1570, I quattro libri dell'architettura
src.loc: Book 3, the Greek palaestra, scan p. 196
src.q: For those prudent men wished—imitating nature, which leads us from one extreme of cold to an extreme of heat by its middle ways—that one should not immediately enter from the cold room into the hot, but by means of the tepid one.

s: Oribasius (in Rasario's Latin) warns against bathing the squeamish or those prone to vomiting, for fear of a stomachic fainting, and those bleeding heavily from the nose; once the illness is concocted the bath can be used safely and helps to bring up phlegm in pleurisy and pneumonia.

src.l: Oribasius, Giovanni Battista Rasario (Latin tr.), 1555, Oribasii Sardiani Collectorum medicinalium libri XVII (Latin tr. Rasario)
src.loc: Collectanea, on bathing the sick, scan p. 349
src.q: Iam nec fastidiosos, nec vomitui obnoxios par est lauare. nam ne hi quoque repente resoluantur, est metus, ita ut syncopa, quae stomachica dicitur, consequatur.

s: For a wasted patient fed on milk, Galen allows a second bath four or five equinoctial hours after the first and a third if he is used to bathing often, 'for these both enjoy and benefit from bathing often', and has him anointed with oil after every bath before he dresses.

src.q: all who bathe must gradually enter the bath chambers. They should not stay in the hot room except as much as is needed to benefit from the resolution of waste and the preparation of the body for food

s: Ibn Sina warns the bather against drinking anything actually cold straight after leaving the bath, because the pores are then open and the cold would reach the principal organs.

src.l: Ibn Sina, 1593, Kitab al-Qanun fi al-tibb (Rome, Medici press, 1593)
src.loc: Qanun, Book 1, fann 3, ta'lim 2, fasl 5, scan p. 91

s: Opening his chapter on the baths of Cairo, al-Maqrizi quotes the lexicographers: istihmam is washing with hot water, and the greeting said to a man leaving the bath, 'tāba ḥammuka', means 'may your sweat be good', a wish for health, since a healthy man's sweat is good.

src.l: al-Maqrizi, 1853, al-Mawa'iz wa-al-i'tibar bi-dhikr al-khitat wa-al-athar (Bulaq, 1853), vol. 2
src.loc: Khitat, 'Dhikr al-hammamat', printed p. 79-80, scan p. 85
src.q: والاستحمام الاغتسال بالماء الحار وقيل هو الاغتسال بأي ما كان والحيم العرق … واما قولهم اذا دخل الحمام اذا خرج طاب حمك فقد يعنى به العرق اي طاب عرقك واذا دعي له بطيب العرق قد دعي له بالصحة لان الصحيح يطيب عرقه

s: Al-Maqrizi cites Muhammad ibn Ishaq that the first to make baths and to use the nūra depilatory was Solomon son of David, and that when he entered and felt its heat he said 'Alas, from the punishment of God, alas'.

src.l: al-Maqrizi, 1853, al-Mawa'iz wa-al-i'tibar bi-dhikr al-khitat wa-al-athar (Bulaq, 1853), vol. 2

s: Al-Maqrizi gathers counts of bath-houses: al-Quda'i's 1,170 in Fustat, nearly eighty in Cairo by the end of 685 AH (1286 CE), and never fewer than a thousand in Baghdad under the caliphs al-Nasir and al-Mustansir.

src.q: citing the Judge al-Quḍāʿī, that there were one thousand one hundred and seventy bathhouses in Fustat of Egypt … the number of bathhouses in Cairo up to the end of the year 685 AH (1286 CE) was nearly eighty. The minimum number of bathhouses in Baghdad during the days of the Caliph al-Nāṣir li-Dīn Allāh and al-Mustanṣir bi-Allāh was one thousand.

s: Al-Maqrizi says the Sabat bath, in his time called the bath of the Mansuri hospital, was for women, and that after Qalawun founded the great hospital it became part of the hospital's endowment.

s: Nasir-i Khusraw (1047) says that at Tiberias a bath-house had been built over a spring beside the Friday mosque, so hot that its water could not be poured over oneself until mixed with cold; people said Solomon built it, and he went in.

src.l: Nasir-i Khusraw, 1881, Safarnama (ed. and French trans. Ch. Schefer, Paris 1881)

src.q: they have built a bathhouse over that spring. The water is so hot that one cannot pour it on oneself until mixing it with cold water. They say this bathhouse was built by Solomon, son of David—peace be upon them. I entered that bathhouse.

s: Arriving in Basra in rags after three months unshorn, Nasir-i Khusraw wanted to go to the bath-house to get warm; he sold his book-bag to put a few dirhams before the bath attendant, who took them for madmen.

src.l: Nasir-i Khusraw, 1881, Safarnama (ed. and French trans. Ch. Schefer, Paris 1881)

src.loc: Safarnama, Basra (1051), Persian text, printed p. 86, scan p. 437
src.q: placed a few black dirhams in a piece of paper to give to the bathhouse attendant, so that he might let us stay a little longer to scrub the grime from ourselves. When I placed those coins before him, he looked at us and thought we were mad.

s: A Shafi'i law manual cites 'A'isha that the Prophet performed, within his washing from janāba, an ablution like that for prayer, and says the sunna is met whether the wuḍū' comes before, during or after the ghusl, though before is best.

s: The same manual counts twenty-one causes for tayammum (dry ablution) and says they are all in truth causes of inability to use water, and that inability is the cause of tayammum.

src.qo: ولداي التيمم اسباب احد وعشرون هي في الحقيقة اسباب للعجز عن استعمال الماء والعجز عن ذلك هو سبب التيمم

s: A Persian satire of women's customs lists the 'rules' of women going to the bath: the waist-cloth (lung) must be put aside while being rubbed with the kīsa and soaped, the head is to be washed with soap three times, and the nūra depilatory should be applied by an adopted sister rather than oneself.

src.l: Aqa Jamal Khwansari (attributed), 1750, Qanun al-nisa' ('Aqa'id al-nisa'), Persian MS 338
src.loc: Qanun al-nisa', fasl dar bayan-i ahkam-i hammam raftan-i zanan, MS p. 30, scan p. 67
src.q: وقت کیسه مالیدن و صابون زدن واجب است که لنگ را از خود دور دارند … و دیگر سر شستن بصابون سه مرتبه واجب میدانند … زنان چون خواهند که نوره کشیدن باید از خواهر خواندگان یکی بگوید که او را بمالد

s: Jurjani explains three kinds of fever by the three ways a bath-house is heated: heat lodged in the walls, stones and bricks (hectic fever), hot water put into the bath's vessels that then warms the walls (humoral fever), and a fire that warms the air of the house (one-day fever).

src.l: Isma'il Jurjani, 1650, Dhakhira-yi Khwarazmshahi, Persian MS 192
src.loc: Dhakhira-yi Khwarazmshahi, Book 5, opening (on fever), scan p. 14
src.q: بجای دیوارها و آجر و سنگ و خشت گرمابه نهاده اند … بجای آب نهاده اند که اندر آوندهای گرمابه ست و ارواح طبعی و حیوانی و نفسانی را و بخارها را که اندر همه تن است بجای هوای گرمابه نهاده اند

s: Lane reports that in Cairo the bath was believed a favourite resort of jinn, so the bather says a short prayer for protection, puts his left foot first over the threshold, and does not pray or recite the Qur'an inside.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1895, An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1895 ed.)
src.loc: Modern Egyptians, ch. 'The Bath', printed p. 350, scan p. 376
src.q: The bath is believed to be a favourite resort of ginn (or genii), and therefore when a person is about to enter it, he should offer up an ejaculatory prayer for protection against evil spirits, and should put his left foot first over the threshold. For the same reason he should not pray nor recite the Kur-án in it.

s: Lane gives the Cairo bath's sequence: the meslakh with raised leewāns and a cold fountain where bathers undress in warm weather; the beyt-owwal, 'first chamber', less warm, used for undressing in winter; then the principal hot room, the harārah, with four leewāns and a hot fountain in the centre.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1895, An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1895 ed.)
src.loc: Modern Egyptians, ch. 'The Bath', printed p. 350, scan p. 376 (the harárah on scan p. 377)
src.q: The first apartment is called the “meslakh.” … In warm weather, the bathers mostly prefer to undress in the meslakh; in winter, they undress in an inner, closed apartment called the “beyt-owwal,”

s: Lane describes the bride's procession (zeffeh) to the bath in Cairo: the whole bath is sometimes hired for the bride and her party, who spend two hours or more washing, playing and feasting, often with hired female singers; back at her family's house the henna is prepared and the guests stick coins in the lump she holds.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1895, An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1895 ed.)
src.loc: Modern Egyptians, ch. 'Marriage', printed p. 178, scan p. 192
src.q: The whole bath is sometimes hired for the bride and her party exclusively. They pass several hours, or seldom less than two, occupied in washing, sporting, and feasting ; and frequently “A'l'mehs” (or female singers) are hired to amuse them in the bath. … a large quantity of henna having been prepared, mixed into a paste, the bride takes a lump of it in her hand, and receives contributions (called “nukoot”) from her guests.

s: In the harārah the operator (mukeyyisātee) cracks almost every joint of the bather, kneads his flesh, and rubs the soles of his feet with a rasp of baked clay.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1895, An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1895 ed.)
src.loc: Modern Egyptians, ch. 'The Bath', printed p. 352, scan p. 378
src.q: The operator cracks almost every joint of his frame: he wrings the body, first one way and then the other, to make several of the vertebræ crack … The mukeyyisátee also kneads the bather’s flesh. After this, or previously, he rubs the soles of his feet with a kind of rasp of baked clay.

s: Lane continues: the flesh is rubbed with a small coarse woollen bag, the bather is lathered with palm fibre (leef) and soap, and then he returns to the beyt-owwal to recline on a mattress with coffee and a pipe for half an hour or an hour while his feet are rubbed.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1895, An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1895 ed.)
src.loc: Modern Egyptians, ch. 'The Bath', printed p. 353, scan p. 379
src.q: The next operation is that of rubbing the bather’s flesh with a small, coarse woollen bag. … lathers the bather with “leef” (or fibres of the palm tree) and soap and sweet water … He generally remains half-an-hour, or an hour, smoking his shibuk or sheesheh; then dresses, and goes out.

s: Lane says the women of Egypt delight in the bath above most pleasures, bring food and their own water, display jewels and talk with friends and strangers; a mother sometimes chooses a bride for her son from the women she sees there; parties hire the khilweh.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1895, An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1895 ed.)
src.loc: Modern Egyptians, ch. 'The Bath', printed p. 354, scan p. 380
src.q: There are few pleasures in which the women of Egypt delight so much as in the visit to the bath, where they frequently have entertainments … Sometimes a mother chooses a bride for her son from among the girls or women whom she chances to see in the bath.

s: Lane says that among the people of Cairo the mother is regarded as ritually impure for a period after childbirth, in most cases forty days (nifās), at the end of which she goes to the bath.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1895, An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1895 ed.)
src.loc: Modern Egyptians, ch. on birth customs, scan p. 539
src.q: During a certain period after childbirth (in most cases, among the people of Cairo, forty days, but differing according to circum- stances, and according to the doctrines of the different sects), the mother is regarded as religiously impure.* The period here men- tioned is called “Nifás.” At the expiration of it the woman goes to the bath.

s: A German account of the Turkish bath (1652) says the attendant washes the bather from two fountains, one warm and one cold, into a marble basin, rubs the soles with a stone, and gives an ointment called Rosma that makes the hair of the private parts fall out.

src.l: Jakob Jost, 1652, Die kleine wunderliche Welt in Türkeyen, Ungarn, Polen (1652)
src.loc: Die kleine wunderliche Welt in Türkeyen, printed p. 104, scan p. 70

s: Qazwini says that at Dawraq in Khuzistan many hot springs visited by the chronically sick collect in two basins, one for men and one for women; whoever goes in briefly benefits, whoever lingers is burned and blistered.

src.q: The water collects in two basins: one for men and the other for women. If one sudden movement enters it briefly, they benefit from it. However, whoever lingers or swims in it will have their body burned and blistered.

s: Qazwini, after Mis'ar ibn Muhalhil, tells of a sick man with an arrowhead grown over in his flesh who stayed three days at a healing spring and was cured, the arrowhead coming out of his side.

src.loc: Athar al-bilad, the spring of Zarawand (Armenia/Azerbaijan), MS scan p. 300

src.loc: Athar al-bilad, the spring of Zarawand (Armenia/Azerbaijan), MS scan p. 300
src.q: He stayed there for three days, and the arrowhead emerged from his side. He was cured of all his other ailments.

s: Ibn Jubayr (1184) was told Baghdad had about two thousand bath-houses on its two banks, most of them coated and levelled with bitumen so that they look like polished black marble, a finish common in the region because bitumen was plentiful from a spring between Basra and Kufa.

src.loc: Rihla, Baghdad (1184), scan p. 193

s: Ibn Jubayr says that in Damascus a poor stranger from the Maghrib could find work watching over a bath-house's service and guarding the clothes of those inside, since only Maghribi strangers were trusted with such posts.

src.l: Ibn Jubayr, 1907, Rihlat Ibn Jubayr (ed. W. Wright, rev. M. J. de Goeje, Leiden 1907)
src.loc: Rihla, Damascus (1184), printed p. 278, scan p. 146

s: Riding to Trapani, Ibn Jubayr passed the fortress of al-Hamma, a large town with many baths fed by springs almost too hot for the body to bear; his party dismounted at one beside the road and rested their bodies by bathing in it.

src.l: Ibn Jubayr, 1907, Rihlat Ibn Jubayr (ed. W. Wright, rev. M. J. de Goeje, Leiden 1907)
src.loc: Rihla, western Sicily near Trapani (Dec. 1184), scan p. 90

src.loc: Rihla, western Sicily near Trapani (Dec. 1184), scan p. 90
src.q: We passed one of them on the road, so we dismounted from the beasts and rested our bodies by bathing in them.

s: Evliya Çelebi heard from the town steward that Tekirdağ had 147 palaces of notables, each with its own private hammam, and confirms that its people use those baths.

src.loc: Seyahatname vol. 8, Tekirdağ (Rodosçuk), printed p. 784, scan p. 15
src.q: there are one hundred and forty-seven palaces within this city, and they say each has its own private hammam.

s: Shirai's Atami guide makes three 'rounds' (三廻り) the rule for a hot-spring cure, regrets that busy visitors stop after one or two, and reports the villagers' saying that by the third round the root of the illness is wholly removed.

src.l: Shirai Tsūki 白井通氣, 1830, 熱海温泉図考 巻之二 (Atami onsen zukō, book 2)
src.loc: 巻之二, 温泉之功験 附浴方, scans 15-16

s: The Atami guide sets the number of soaks by constitution: four or five a day and night for a person of ordinary strength, five or six for the robust, two or three for the weak or sick; more than that does harm.

src.l: Shirai Tsūki 白井通氣, 1830, 熱海温泉図考 巻之二 (Atami onsen zukō, book 2)
src.loc: 巻之二, 入湯の法, scan 10

s: For the first soak the guide says to warm the tub's edge, sit on it with the feet in, scoop water onto the face, wet the body, then enter quietly; in the tub one should not brood but keep the breath (気) even and the heart level, and get out when the heat has gone through the whole body.

src.l: Shirai Tsūki 白井通氣, 1830, 熱海温泉図考 巻之二 (Atami onsen zukō, book 2)
src.loc: 巻之二, 入湯の法, scan 11

s: After the bath, the Atami guide warns, one must not sit in the wind however pleasant it feels; during the cure wine is forbidden, or at least not to excess, and sex is out of the question.

src.l: Shirai Tsūki 白井通氣, 1830, 熱海温泉図考 巻之二 (Atami onsen zukō, book 2)
src.loc: 巻之二, 入湯の法, scan 12

s: Closing his rules (no bathing on an empty stomach or straight after a meal, no cold food or raw flesh), Shirai says that one who regards the hot spring as a god and as a lord, and bathes without slackening in self-care, will find its effect very strong.

src.l: Shirai Tsūki 白井通氣, 1830, 熱海温泉図考 巻之二 (Atami onsen zukō, book 2)
src.loc: 巻之二, 入湯の法, scan 13

s: The guide says people of every rank, from lords' wives down, come to Atami to bathe; the tub is about 4 shaku 5 sun long and over 2 shaku wide, and because the water is too hot to enter it is first run into a holding tank, and a board is lifted to let it flow in until the bath is neither too tepid nor too hot.

src.l: Shirai Tsūki 白井通氣, 1830, 熱海温泉図考 巻之二 (Atami onsen zukō, book 2)
src.loc: 巻之二, scans 4-5

s: The painting of the bathroom at Atami carries a note that the barrel hung above is filled with hot water and its tap opened as a waterfall to strike the head and shoulders.

src.l: Shirai Tsūki 白井通氣, 1830, 熱海温泉図考 巻之二 (Atami onsen zukō, book 2)
src.loc: 巻之二, 浴室之図 (painting), scan 7

s: The stele of Atami's Yuzen shrine, as copied in the guide, says that tradition holds that in 749 the god Sukunahikona possessed a child and said that whoever bathed here would surely be healed of chronic illness, that it came true, and that people then built the shrine.

src.l: Shirai Tsūki 白井通氣, 1830, 熱海温泉図考 巻之二 (Atami onsen zukō, book 2)
src.loc: 巻之二, 湯前神社 stele inscription (1770), scan 22

s: Among Atami's baths Shirai lists the Kawara no yu, a mixed-entry bath (入込の湯) where farmers usually bathe, very dirty, yet so effective that some guests staying at the inns come there on purpose.

src.l: Shirai Tsūki 白井通氣, 1830, 熱海温泉図考 巻之一 (Atami onsen zukō, book 1)
src.loc: 巻之一, 熱海市中, scan 69

s: Quoting a book on the principles of hot springs, Shirai's guide says Chinese hot springs are fierce and Japan's gentle, because Japan is a country where yin and yang are evenly balanced and its springs receive a well-tempered qi.

src.l: Shirai Tsūki 白井通氣, 1830, 熱海温泉図考 巻之一 (Atami onsen zukō, book 1)
src.loc: 巻之一, scans 28-30

s: Motoi's health manual (1812) answers people who will not take a furo bath because they think it poisonous: hot springs cure illnesses, there are medicinal baths taken in the furo, and the bath taken in moderation makes qi and blood circulate.

src.l: Motoi Shishō 本井子承, 1812, 長命衛生論 下 (Chōmei eiseiron, vol. 3)
src.loc: 下之巻, 風呂に浴心得の事, scans 67-68

s: The manual lists what to avoid in the furo: bathing after a big meal, on an empty stomach or straight after eating, when very drunk, entering very hot or tepid water, going in straight from the wind, staying in long, talking loudly in the bath; and, unless it is a medicinal bath, entering several times a day.

src.l: Motoi Shishō 本井子承, 1812, 長命衛生論 下 (Chōmei eiseiron, vol. 3)
src.loc: 下之巻, 風呂に浴心得の事, scan 68

s: At the furo or a tub wash (行水), the manual says, soak a towel in hot water and pour it from the shoulders down the back again and again; with no furo, wring the towel and rub from the shoulders to the chest, so that the blood circulates.

src.l: Motoi Shishō 本井子承, 1812, 長命衛生論 (Chōmei eiseiron, vol. 4)
src.loc: vol. 4, scan 36

s: Katsuki says that in Japan the newborn is bathed (産湯) as soon as the cord is cut, and that the place of the birth bath should be shut with doors and screens so that no wind gets in.

src.l: Katsuki Gyūzan 香月牛山, 1714, 小児必用養育草 巻一 (Shōni hitsuyō sodategusa, vol. 1)
src.loc: 巻一, 四 児子取擧様の説, scans 24-25

s: Katsuki notes that in China the newborn is first washed on the third day, while recent Japanese custom bathes it at once; and that the Shūgaishō lists lucky days for a newborn's first bath, with water drawn from a stream flowing east.

src.l: Katsuki Gyūzan 香月牛山, 1714, 小児必用養育草 巻一 (Shōni hitsuyō sodategusa, vol. 1)
src.loc: 巻一, 産湯の説, scan 35

s: In a case history, Katsuki says that a crippled child, after a year of pills, soaked at the Tawarayama hot spring in Nagato for three times seven days and became whole.

src.l: Katsuki Gyūzan 香月牛山, 1714, 小児必用養育草 巻三 (Shōni hitsuyō sodategusa, vol. 3)
src.loc: 巻三, scan 36

s: Katsuki describes a Japanese custom of bathing a child with heated rice-washing water (米泔水), sometimes with a little sake added, when the smallpox scabs have formed; measles and chickenpox are treated the same way, and the child is then kept from wind and cold.

src.l: Katsuki Gyūzan 香月牛山, 1714, 小児必用養育草 巻五 (Shōni hitsuyō sodategusa, vol. 5)
src.loc: 巻五, scans 10 and 40

s: The Nihon saijiki (1688) records the popular custom of bathing in iris water (菖蒲湯) on the fifth day of the fifth month, and traces it to Chinese texts on bathing in orchid water that day.

src.l: Kaibara Yoshifuru (Chiken) 貝原好古, Kaibara Ekiken (ed.), 1688, 日本歳時記 巻五 (Nihon saijiki, vol. 5)
src.loc: 巻五, 五月五日, scan 22

s: For high summer the Nihon saijiki quotes a Chinese health book: in great heat even washing the hands in cold water withers the five organs, so bathing in it must be strictly forbidden.

src.l: Kaibara Yoshifuru (Chiken) 貝原好古, Kaibara Ekiken (ed.), 1688, 日本歳時記 巻五 (Nihon saijiki, vol. 5)
src.loc: 巻五, 夏 (quoting 寿養養書), scan 5

s: Nasu's notes on Japanese medicine say hot springs are bathed in for women's cold loins and discharge, and that for those too far from a spring to travel an artificial hot spring is made to bathe in.

src.l: Nasu Tsunenori 奈須恒徳, 1824, 本朝医談 (Honchō idan)
src.loc: scan 64

s: The 1790 government first-aid manual has an entry for fainting in the bath after soaking long or in very hot water: spray cold water on the face or over the body, then give salt water or a cup of vinegar.

src.l: Taki Motonori 多紀元徳 (ed.), 1790, 広恵済急方 上 (Kōkeisai kyūhō, vol. 1)
src.loc: 上, 入浴倒, scan 201

s: The Konjaku tale of the long-nosed priest of Ike-no-o says that his temple was so prosperous that in its bath-house (湯屋) the monks heated water and bathed every day.

src.l: Anonymous, 1120, 今昔物語集 (Konjaku monogatari shū), modern printed edition
src.loc: 巻28 第20 (池尾禅珍内供鼻語), printed p. 1293, scan 302

src.loc: 巻28 第20 (池尾禅珍内供鼻語), printed p. 1293, scan 302

s: The Man'yōshū has a poem by Yamabe no Akahito made at the Iyo hot spring; the editor's note adds that the Nihon shoki records the Iyo spring sinking and ceasing to flow after the earthquake of Tenmu 13 (684).

s: The Bungo fudoki says that after a great earthquake in Tenmu's reign hot springs broke out on Mount Itsuma, steam hot enough to cook rice fast, and that one well-like spring of deep indigo water, which does not flow, surges up more than a fathom when it hears a human voice: it is called the 'angry spring' (慍湯).

src.l: Tsukamoto Tetsuzō (ed.), 1915, 古事記・風土記 (Kojiki with the fudoki), ed. Tsukamoto Tetsuzō
src.loc: 豊後國風土記, 日田郡 五馬山, printed p. 575, scan 18

src.q: The steam was so hot that rice could be cooked quickly. … There is one hot spring whose hole resembles a well. It is over one fathom deep, and the depth is unknown. The color of the water is like indigo.
src.qo: ゆけむり湯氣あつくさかりに熾熱。はやくなりぬ炊飯早熟。

s: The Heike says the monk Mongaku went under the Nachi waterfall in the twelfth month, among snow and icicles, stood in its pool up to the neck reciting the Jikushu spell, vowed to be struck by the falls for three times seven days, and when he went back the falling water felt like hot water.

src.l: Anonymous, Yamada Takao (ed.), 1371, 平家物語 (The Tale of the Heike), vol. 2
src.loc: 巻五, 文覺荒行, scans 18-19
src.q: 比は十二月十日餘の事なれば、雪降積り、つららいて … 文覺瀑下に下 浸り、頸際漬て、慈救の咒を誦するが … 我 此瀑に三七日打れて、慈救の三洛叉を誦うと思ふ大願有り

s: Bashō writes that at Iizaka there was a hot spring, so he bathed and then looked for lodging, which turned out to be a poor house with mats on an earth floor, where rain leaked and fleas and mosquitoes kept him awake.

src.l: Matsuo Bashō, 1694, おくのほそ道 (Oku no hosomichi) with supplements (補遺)
src.loc: Iizaka (飯塚), scan 10

s: In a prose fragment printed in the supplement, Bashō says he bathed at Yamanaka in Kaga, which the villagers call one of Japan's three famous springs, and that the water soaked the skin, reached the sinews and bones, and loosened the spirit.

s: Ekiken's handbook of numbered lists gives 'the number of bathing days': except in summer, wash the hair every five days and the body every ten; frequent bathing feels pleasant outside but disperses and leaks qi inside.

src.l: Kaibara Ekiken, 1910, 益軒全集 (Ekiken zenshū), vol. 2
src.loc: 續和漢名數, 沐浴日數 (citing 洞虛子), scan 918

src.loc: 續和漢名數, 沐浴日數 (citing 洞虛子), scan 918
src.q: If one bathes frequently, the exterior feels adjusted and smooth, but the interior actually disperses qi and leaks.

s: Ham Chin-sung's record of the Diamond Mountains says the Onjŏng pass takes its name from a hot spring at its foot, five li from the monastery (Sin'gye-sa); the monks dredged and widened it, made two baths (兩湯) and roofed them, and set a stone bench in each so that one can sit to bathe.

src.l: Ham Chin-sung 咸鎭嵩, 1850, 金剛遊記 (Kŭmgang yugi, Records of travel in the Diamond Mountains)
src.loc: 溫井嶺, scan 40

s: In the same passage an official complains that the Sin'gye spring is not hot enough and praises the P'yŏngsan spring, whose sand one cannot hold in the hand; Ham answers that a spring that hot is wasted, since the value of a hot spring is that it suits bathing: if no one can scoop its sand, who will bathe in it, unless you want to boil chickens? The Sin'gye water is 'just right'.
