s: King Yŏngjo writes that after bathing at the hot spring in the autumn of 1750 he was almost cured; when the complaint returned in high summer, carrying spring water would burden the people, so he had the palace medical office boil sulphur into water, since the Onjŏng (Onyang) water contains sulphur; it smelled like the spring and had the same nature, and in a poem he gives a jar of it to his ministers in place of their own journeys to bathe.

s: Pak Chong-gyŏm records that in the seventh month of 1760 the Crown Prince (Sado) went to bathe at the hot spring; the king had at first refused, so the prince showed his officials his swollen feet, for he had damp sores, and so got leave to go; the journey set out on the 18th after days of flood rain.

s: Kang Kyo-sŏk's travel poems describe the Onjŏng (also called Talch'ŏn) in Ch'ori-bang: water boiling up between rocks, steaming like a hot stove, which 'not only removes dirt but bathes illness away'; he writes a poem for each of its 'three baths' (題三湯): the men's bath, the women's bath, where girls bathe together, wash clothes and hair and look in the mirror, and a 'dripping-water bath' where warm water falls in a stream 'not a waterfall, but like one'.

s: Kim Chang-saeng's ritual answers take up washing the dead: asked why people now wash the corpse in water of fragrant wood, and whether hair should be washed in rice-water (潘) as the classics say, he answers that fragrant water appears in the Five Rites only for the king's funeral, so to use it would be presumption; the hair-washing water should follow the classics and be rice-water.

s: The Agni Purāṇa's daily bath for the Śaiva worshipper comes in two stages: first a 'dirt bath' (malasnāna), with earth dug from eight fingers deep and divided in three, one part to wash from navel to feet, another for the whole body, then submerging with mouth and eyes closed and breath held; then the 'rule bath' (vidhisnāna), standing navel-deep facing north, drawing the holy fords (tīrtha) into the water with a hand gesture, plunging while remembering Śiva, Hari or the Ganges, and finishing with fragrant amalaka and other 'royal' toilet articles.

s: The same chapter lists baths without immersion: an ash bath (bhasmasnāna) rubbed from head to foot; a 'Mahendra' bath standing face-east with arms raised when rain falls in sunshine; a bath in the dust thrown up by the hooves of a herd of cows; a 'mantra bath' of sprinkling; and a 'mental bath' (mānasa snāna) made with breath-control and the root mantra, 'prescribed everywhere'.

s: For the king's Puṣya bath (puṣyasnāna), Varāhamihira sets a separate 'bath altar' west of the main altar; strong pots with white thread round their necks, covered with leaves and fruit of milky-sap trees, stand at its corners, filled with water mixed with the Puṣya-bath ingredients and gems; following Garga he lists the herbs to go in them (jyotiṣmatī, abhayā, śatāvarī, brāhmī and others), with all seeds, gold and perfumes.

s: On the bath altar are spread four hides in order (an old bull that died of age, a fighting bull, a lion, a tiger), and on them a 'auspicious seat' (bhadrāsana) of gold, silver, copper or milky-sap wood, one, one and a quarter, or one and a half cubits high; the king sits on it among ministers, priest and astrologer while bards, citizens and brahmins shout and drums, conches and trumpets sound.

s: The Mahābhārata's pilgrimage catalogue prices each ford in sacrifices: at Naimiṣa, where 'whatever fords there are on earth' are present, the pilgrim should stay a month, and one who has bathed there (kṛtābhiṣeka), self-restrained and keeping a restricted diet, gains the fruit of a cow-sacrifice and purifies his family to the seventh generation; bathing at Gopratāra on the Sarayū, at Rāmatīrtha on the Gomatī, or in the Kapila pool at Vārāṇasī earns heaven, a horse sacrifice, or a rājasūya.

s: In the Vinaya rules for the monks' hot bath-room (jantāghara), the Buddha allows a brick facing for the damp lower wall and a chimney, places the fire at one side of a small bath-room and in the middle of a large one, and, when the fire scorched their faces, allows clay to spread over the face, with a trough to moisten it in.

s: When the fire scorched their bodies the monks were allowed to have water poured over them, from a water stand with saucers; a thatched bath-room 'did not produce perspiration', so its roof was to be covered and plastered inside and out; the floor was to be brick, stone or wood, washed, and given a drain.

s: Naked monks may not salute, serve, give, eat or drink; but since they then feared to help one another in the bath, the Buddha allows 'three kinds of coverings: the covering of the bath-room, the covering of the water, and the covering by clothes', within which service (bathing and shampooing) is permitted; a bamboo or string is allowed for hanging robes, and a well for the bath-room's water.

s: A Tibetan medical commentary defines the hot spring (chu tshan) by touch: water whose substance has the tactile nature of fire; even if not made by human effort, any water hot to the touch is a hot spring. It explains the springs by black coal-stone (rdo sol) meeting water underground: more or less coal gives more or less heat.

s: The commentary sets the course of a soak: begin with the cooler water and, once used to it, stay in progressively hotter; on coming out cover the body with thick clothes and, if there is warm ground, lie on it, much steaming sweat being best; sessions are short at first and lengthened, then shortened again at the end; for weak patients a month or half a month is best; and for the healthy, bathing in the best springs in the four seasons keeps illness away.

s: The rGyud bzhi's chapter on medicinal baths (lums) lists who may bathe (stiff or contracted limbs, old wounds, all wind diseases) and who may not (infectious fever, jaundice, the weak); it forbids applying baths to the eyes, cheeks, testicles, abdomen and heart region; and it gives two methods, the 'water bath' (chu lums), which is made of natural hot springs, and the 'binding bath' (bcing lums); where no spring is to be had, a bath of the 'five ambrosias' (bdud rtsi lnga) or a steam bath replaces it.
